title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: "Here it comes again! Again I see it all!" Anna said to herself, the moment the carriage moved off and, swaying lightly, began rumbling over the little paving stones of the road, and once again one impression chased rapidly after another.

"Yes — what was the last thing I was thinking about so clearly?" she tried to remember. "'_Tiutkin, coiffeur?_' — no, not that. Yes, what Yashvin says, that the struggle for existence and hatred are the one thing that holds people together. No, it's a useless trip you're making," she said in her head to a party in a coach and four, evidently off on an outing in the country. "And the dog you're taking along will be no use to you. You can't get away from yourselves." Turning her eyes in the direction Pyotr had glanced, she saw a factory worker who was almost dead drunk, his head hanging, being led off by a policeman. "There — he's found a quicker way," she thought. "Count Vronsky and I didn't find that happiness either, even though we expected so much from it." And now, for the first time, Anna turned the glaring light in which she was seeing everything onto her relationship with him, which she had been avoiding thinking about until now. "What was he looking for in me? Not love so much as the gratification of vanity." She remembered his words, the expression on his face, like an abject setter, in the early days of their affair. And everything now confirmed it. "Yes, there was the thrill of conquest in him. Of course there was love too, but the main element was the pride of having pulled it off. He showed me off. Now that's over. There's nothing to be proud of. Not to be proud of, but to be ashamed of. He's taken from me everything he could, and now I'm no use to him. He's tired of me, and he's trying not to behave dishonorably toward me. He let it slip yesterday — he wants the divorce and the marriage so he can burn his bridges. He loves me, but how? The zest is gone, as the English say. That fellow there wants everyone to admire him and is very pleased with himself," she thought, looking at a red-faced clerk riding a riding-school horse. "Yes, there's no flavor left in me for him now. If I leave him, deep down he'll be glad."
This wasn't just a guess; she saw it distinctly in the piercing light that was now revealing the meaning of life and of human relationships to her.

"My love keeps growing more passionate and selfish, while his keeps fading and fading, and that's why we're drifting apart." She went on thinking. "And there's no helping it. He is everything for me, and I want him more and more to give himself over to me completely. And he wants more and more to get away from me. We walked toward each other right up to the point of falling in love, and ever since we've been irresistibly drifting in opposite directions. And nothing can change that. He tells me I'm insanely jealous, and I've told myself the same thing; but it isn't true. I'm not jealous, I'm dissatisfied. But...." She parted her lips and shifted in her seat in the excitement of the thought that had just struck her. "If only I could be something other than a mistress, caring passionately about nothing but his caresses; but I can't, and I don't want to be anything else. And by that very wanting I provoke disgust in him, and he provokes rage in me, and it can't be any different. Don't I know that he wouldn't deceive me, that he has no designs on Princess Sorokina, that he isn't in love with Kitty, that he won't desert me! I know all that, but it doesn't make it any better. If, without loving me, he treats me well and kindly out of _duty_, and doesn't give me what I want, that's a thousand times worse than unkindness! That's — hell! And that's exactly how it is. For a long time now he hasn't loved me. And where love ends, hate begins. I don't know these streets at all. Hills, it seems, and still houses and more houses.... And in the houses, always people and more people.... How many of them, no end of them, and all hating each other! Come on, let me try to think what it would take to make me happy. Well? Suppose I get a divorce, and Alexey Alexandrovitch lets me have Seryozha, and I marry Vronsky." Thinking of Alexey Alexandrovitch, she at once pictured him with extraordinary clarity, as if he were alive in front of her, with his mild, lifeless, dull eyes, the blue veins on his white hands, his intonations and the cracking of his fingers, and remembering the feeling that had existed between them, which had also been called love, she shuddered with revulsion. "All right, I'm divorced, and I become Vronsky's wife. Well, will Kitty stop looking at me the way she looked at me today? No. And will Seryozha stop asking about and wondering at my two husbands? And is there any new feeling I could awaken between Vronsky and me? Is there any chance, if not of happiness, then at least of some relief from misery? No, no!" she answered now without any hesitation at all. "Impossible! Life is pulling us apart, and I'm the cause of his unhappiness and he of mine, and there's no changing him or me. Every attempt has been made — the screw has been stripped. Oh, a beggar woman with a baby. She thinks I'll feel sorry for her. Aren't we all just flung into the world to hate each other, and so to torture ourselves and each other? Schoolboys coming — laughing Seryozha?" she thought. "I imagined I loved him too, and used to be moved by my own tenderness. But I've lived without him, I traded him for another love, and didn't regret the trade until that love was satisfied." And with disgust she thought about what she had meant by that love. And the clarity with which she now saw life, her own and everyone else's, was a pleasure to her. "It's the same with me and Pyotr, and the coachman Fyodor, and that merchant, and all the people living along the Volga where those posters invite you to go, and everywhere, and always," she thought, just as she had pulled in under the low-pitched roof of the Nizhigorod station and the porters came running to meet her.
"A ticket to Obiralovka?" Pyotr said.
She had completely forgotten where she was going and why, and only with great effort grasped the question.
"Yes," she said, handing him her purse, and taking a little red bag in her hand, she got out of the carriage.

Pushing her way through the crowd to the first-class waiting room, she gradually remembered every detail of her situation, and the plans she was wavering between. And once again, in the same old sore spots, hope and then despair poisoned the wounds of her tortured, fearfully hammering heart. Sitting on the star-shaped sofa waiting for the train, she looked with disgust at the people coming and going (they were all hateful to her) and thought about how she would get to the station, how she would write him a note, what she would write, and how he was right now complaining to his mother about his position, not understanding her suffering, and how she would walk into the room and what she would say. Then she thought that life might still be happy, and how miserably she loved and hated him, and how terribly her heart was pounding.

title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: A bell rang; some young men, ugly and brash and at the same time careful of the impression they were making, hurried past. Pyotr too crossed the room in his livery and top boots, with his dull, animal face, and came up to take her to the train. Some noisy men went quiet as she passed them on the platform, and one whispered something about her to another — something nasty, no doubt. She stepped up onto the high step and sat down by herself in a compartment, on a dirty seat that had once been white. Her bag lay next to her, jolted up and down by the springiness of the seat. With a stupid smile Pyotr lifted his hat, with its colored band, to her at the window, in farewell; an insolent conductor slammed the door and threw the latch. A grotesque-looking lady in a bustle (Anna mentally stripped her and was horrified at how hideous she was) and a little girl laughing affectedly ran down the platform.
"Katerina Andreevna, she's got them all, _ma tante!_" the little girl shouted.

"Even the child is ugly and affected," Anna thought. To avoid having to see anyone, she got up quickly and sat down by the opposite window of the empty compartment. A misshapen peasant, covered in dirt, in a cap from which his tangled hair stuck out all around, walked past that window, bending down toward the carriage wheels. "There's something familiar about that hideous peasant," Anna thought. And remembering her dream, she moved over to the opposite door, shaking with terror. The conductor opened the door and let in a husband and wife.
"Would you like to get out?"

Anna didn't answer. The conductor and her two new fellow passengers did not see her panic-stricken face under her veil. She went back to her corner and sat down. The couple settled themselves on the opposite side and intently but discreetly looked over her clothes. Both husband and wife seemed repulsive to Anna. The husband asked whether she would mind if he smoked, plainly not because he actually wanted to smoke but because he wanted to start a conversation with her. When she said it was fine, he said to his wife in French something about preferring talking to smoking. They exchanged inane, affected remarks with one another, entirely for her benefit. Anna saw clearly that they were sick of each other and that they hated each other. And no one could have helped hating such pathetic monstrosities.

A second bell rang, followed by the moving of luggage, noise, shouting, and laughter. It was so plain to Anna that there was nothing for anyone to be glad about that this laughter grated on her painfully, and she wanted to plug her ears so she wouldn't have to hear it. Finally the third bell rang, there was a whistle and a hiss of steam and a clank of chains, and the man in her compartment crossed himself. "It would be interesting to ask him what he means by that," Anna thought, looking at him angrily. She looked past the lady out the window at the people who seemed to be spinning past as they ran beside the train or stood on the platform. The train, jolting at regular intervals at the joints of the rails, rolled past the platform, past a stone wall, a signal box, past other trains; the wheels, moving more smoothly and evenly, rang faintly on the rails. The window was lit up by the bright evening sun, and a slight breeze tugged at the curtain. Anna forgot her fellow passengers, and to the gentle rocking of the train she began thinking again, breathing in the fresh air.

"Yes, where did I leave off? That I couldn't picture a situation in which life would not be misery, that we are all created to be miserable, and that we all know it, and we all invent ways of fooling each other. And when you see the truth, what are you supposed to do?"
"That's what reason is given to a person for — to escape from what bothers him," said the lady in French, lisping affectedly, and obviously pleased with her own phrase.
The words seemed like an answer to Anna's thoughts.

"To escape from what bothers him," Anna repeated. And glancing at the red-cheeked husband and the thin wife, she saw that the sickly wife considered herself misunderstood, and that the husband cheated on her and encouraged her in that self-image. Anna seemed to see their entire history and all the recesses of their souls, as if she were turning a light on them. But there was nothing interesting in them, and she went back to her own train of thought.

"Yes, I'm very much bothered, and that's what reason was given to me for — to escape; so then I have to escape. Why not put out the light, when there's nothing left worth looking at, when looking at it all has become sickening? But how? Why is the conductor running along the footboard, why are they shrieking, those young men in that train? Why are they talking, why are they laughing? It's all falsehood, all lying, all humbug, all cruelty!..."

When the train pulled into the station, Anna stepped out into the crowd of passengers, and moving away from them as if they were lepers, she stood on the platform, trying to think what she had come here for and what she meant to do. Everything that had seemed possible to her before now felt impossibly hard to consider, especially in this noisy crowd of ugly people who wouldn't leave her alone. One moment porters were running up to her, offering their services; the next, young men, clattering their heels on the planks of the platform and talking loudly, were staring at her; people coming the other way dodged her on the wrong side. Remembering that she had intended to go on further if there was no answer, she stopped a porter and asked if her coachman wasn't here with a note from Count Vronsky.
"Count Vronsky? They sent up here from the Vronskys just a moment ago, to meet Princess Sorokina and her daughter. What does the coachman look like?"

Just as she was talking to the porter, the coachman Mihail, red-faced and cheerful in his smart blue coat and chain, evidently proud of having carried out his errand so successfully, came up to her and handed her a letter. She tore it open, and her heart ached before she had read it.
"I am very sorry your note didn't reach me. I'll be home at ten," Vronsky had written carelessly....
"Yes, that's exactly what I expected!" she said to herself with a bitter smile.

"Very well, you can go home then," she said softly to Mihail. She spoke softly because her heart was pounding so fast it was hard to breathe. "No, I won't let you make me miserable," she thought menacingly, addressing not him, not herself, but the power that was making her suffer, and she walked along the platform.

Two maidservants walking along the platform turned their heads to look at her and made some remark about her dress. "Real," they said about the lace she was wearing. The young men wouldn't leave her alone. They came past again, looking into her face, and with a laugh shouting something in unnatural voices. The stationmaster came up and asked if she was taking the train. A boy selling kvas couldn't take his eyes off her. "My God! Where am I to go?" she thought, walking farther and farther along the platform. At the end she stopped. Some ladies and children, who had come to meet a gentleman in spectacles, broke off their loud laughter and chatter and stared at her as she reached them. She picked up her pace and moved away from them to the edge of the platform. A freight train was coming in. The platform started to shake, and she felt as though she were on the train again.

And all at once she remembered the man crushed by the train the day she had first met Vronsky, and she knew what she had to do. With quick, light steps she went down the stairs that led from the water tank to the rails, and stopped right beside the approaching train.

She looked at the lower part of the carriages, at the bolts and chains and the tall cast-iron wheel of the front carriage as it slowly rolled toward her, and tried to gauge the midpoint between the front and back wheels, and the exact instant when that midpoint would be opposite her.

"There," she said to herself, looking into the shadow under the carriage at the sand and coal dust covering the sleepers — "there, right in the middle, and I'll punish him and get away from everyone and from myself."

She tried to throw herself under the wheels of the first carriage as it came up to her; but the red bag she was trying to drop from her hand held her back, and she was too late — she missed the moment. She had to wait for the next carriage. A feeling like the one she used to have when she was about to take her first plunge into the water came over her, and she crossed herself. That familiar gesture brought a whole flood of girlish and childish memories back to her soul, and suddenly the darkness that had covered everything for her was torn open, and life rose up in front of her for an instant with all its bright past joys. But she didn't take her eyes off the wheels of the second carriage. And at the precise instant when the gap between the wheels came opposite her, she dropped the red bag, drew her head down into her shoulders, fell on her hands under the carriage, and lightly, as though she were about to get up again at once, dropped onto her knees. And at the same moment she was struck with horror at what she was doing. "Where am I? What am I doing? What for?" She tried to get up, to fall back; but something huge and pitiless struck her on the head and rolled her onto her back. "Lord, forgive me everything!" she said, feeling that struggling was impossible. A peasant, muttering to himself, was working on the iron above her. And the light by which she had read the book filled with troubles, lies, sorrow, and evil flared up brighter than ever before, lit up for her everything that had been in darkness, flickered, began to fade, and was put out forever.
PART EIGHT

title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: Nearly two months had gone by. The hot summer was half over, but Sergey Ivanovitch was only just getting ready to leave Moscow.

Sergey Ivanovitch's life had not been uneventful during this time. A year earlier he had finished his book, the product of six years' work, "Sketch of a Survey of the Principles and Forms of Government in Europe and Russia." Several sections of the book and its introduction had appeared in journals, and other parts had been read aloud by Sergey Ivanovitch to people in his own circle, so that the leading ideas in the work could not be completely new to the public. Even so, Sergey Ivanovitch had been counting on its publication to make a serious impression on society, and, if it did not cause a revolution in social science, at the very least to make a major stir in the academic world.
After the most painstaking revision, the book had been published the previous year and distributed to the booksellers.

Though he asked no one about it, answered his friends' inquiries about how the book was doing with reluctance and feigned indifference, and didn't even ask the booksellers how it was selling, Sergey Ivanovitch was watching with strained attention, on high alert for the first impression his book would make in society and in the literary world.

But a week passed, then another, then a third, and no impression at all could be detected in society. His specialist and academic friends occasionally — unmistakably out of politeness — mentioned it. The rest of his acquaintances, not interested in a book on a scholarly subject, didn't bring it up at all. And society in general — particularly absorbed at the moment in other things — was completely indifferent. In the press, too, for a whole month not a word about his book.
Sergey Ivanovitch had calculated the time required to write a review down to the day, but a month passed, and a second, and there was still silence.

Only in the _Northern Beetle_, in a comic piece on the singer Drabanti, who had lost his voice, was there a dismissive jab at Koznishev's book, suggesting that everyone had seen through it long ago and that it was a subject of general ridicule.
Finally, in the third month, a critical article appeared in a serious review. Sergey Ivanovitch knew its author. He had met him once at Golubtsov's.
The author of the article was a young man, an invalid, very bold as a writer but extremely deficient in breeding and shy in person.
Despite his absolute contempt for the author, Sergey Ivanovitch sat down to read the piece with complete respect. The article was devastating.

The critic had quite clearly imposed on the book an interpretation it could not possibly bear. But he had picked his quotations so skillfully that to anyone who hadn't read the book (and almost nobody had read it) it seemed perfectly obvious that the whole thing was nothing but a jumble of high-flown phrases, not even — as the question marks suggested — used in the right places, and that the author of the book was a person with no knowledge of his subject whatsoever. And it was all done so wittily that Sergey Ivanovitch wouldn't have minded owning the wit himself. And that was precisely what was so terrible.

However scrupulously Sergey Ivanovitch verified the correctness of the critic's arguments, he did not stop for a minute to dwell on the supposed flaws and mistakes that were being mocked; but unconsciously he began at once trying to recall every detail of his meeting and conversation with the article's author.
"Did I offend him in some way?" Sergey Ivanovitch wondered.
And remembering that during their meeting he had corrected the young man on something he had said that betrayed ignorance, Sergey Ivanovitch found the key to the article.

This article was followed by a deadly silence about the book, both in the press and in conversation, and Sergey Ivanovitch saw that the six years' work he had labored at with such love and effort had vanished without a trace.

Sergey Ivanovitch's position was made even more difficult by the fact that, since finishing his book, he no longer had any literary work to do of the kind that had taken up most of his time until then.

Sergey Ivanovitch was intelligent, cultivated, healthy, and energetic, and he did not know what to do with his energy. Drawing-room conversations, meetings, assemblies, and committees — wherever there was talk to be had — took up some of his time. But long used to city life, he didn't burn off all his energies in talk, the way his less experienced younger brother did when he was in Moscow. He still had a great deal of free time and intellectual energy to spare.

Luckily for him, at this period that was so hard for him because of the failure of his book, the various public questions — the dissenting sects, the American alliance, the Samara famine, exhibitions, spiritualism — were definitively replaced in the public mind by the Slavonic question, which up to then had only mildly interested society, and Sergey Ivanovitch, who had been one of the first to take up this subject, threw himself into it heart and soul.

In the circle Sergey Ivanovitch belonged to, nothing was talked about or written about just now except the Servian War. Everything the idle public ordinarily does to kill time was now done for the benefit of the Slavonic states. Balls, concerts, dinners, matchboxes, ladies' dresses, beer, restaurants — everything testified to sympathy with the Slavonic peoples.

On many of the things being said and written on the subject Sergey Ivanovitch disagreed at various points. He could see that the Slavonic question had turned into one of those fashionable distractions that take turns providing society with an object and an occupation. He could see, too, that a great many people were taking it up out of self-interest and self-promotion. He recognized that the newspapers were printing a lot that was superfluous and exaggerated, with the sole purpose of attracting attention and outdoing one another. He could see that in this general movement the people who pushed themselves forward most and shouted loudest were men who had failed and were nursing a grievance — generals without armies, ministers out of the ministry, journalists without a paper, party leaders without followers. He could see that there was a great deal in it that was frivolous and absurd. But he could see and recognize an unmistakable, growing enthusiasm, uniting all classes, that it was impossible not to sympathize with. The slaughter of men who were fellow Christians and of the same Slavonic blood stirred up sympathy for the victims and outrage against the oppressors. And the heroism of the Servians and Montenegrins fighting for a great cause produced in the people as a whole a longing to help their brothers not in words but in deeds.

But there was another side to this that delighted Sergey Ivanovitch: the manifestation of public opinion. The public had clearly expressed its will. The soul of the people, as Sergey Ivanovitch put it, had found expression. And the more he worked in this cause, the more incontestable it became to him that this was a cause destined to take on vast dimensions, to mark an epoch.

He threw himself heart and soul into the service of this great cause and forgot to think about his book. His whole time was now taken up with it, so that he could barely manage to keep up with all the letters and appeals addressed to him. He worked the entire spring and part of the summer, and it was only in July that he finally got ready to go to his brother's in the country.

He was going both to rest for a fortnight, and, in the very heart of the people, in the most remote backwoods, to enjoy the spectacle of that uplifting of the people's spirit which he, like every resident of the capital and big cities, was fully convinced of. Katavasov had long meant to make good on his promise to visit Levin, so he was going with him.

title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: Sergey Ivanovitch and Katavasov had only just reached the station of the Kursk line, which was unusually busy and packed with people that day, when, looking around for the groom who was following with their luggage, they saw a party of volunteers driving up in four cabs. Ladies met them with bouquets of flowers, and followed by the surging crowd they all went into the station.
One of the ladies who had been meeting the volunteers came out of the hall and addressed Sergey Ivanovitch.
"You're here to see them off too?" she asked in French.
"No, I'm leaving myself, princess. Going to my brother's for a break. Do you always come to see them off?" said Sergey Ivanovitch with a barely visible smile.
"Oh, it would be impossible not to!" the princess answered. "Is it true that eight hundred have already been sent from us? Malvinsky wouldn't believe me."
"More than eight hundred. If you count those who weren't sent directly from Moscow, over a thousand," Sergey Ivanovitch answered.
"There! That's just what I said!" the lady exclaimed. "And is it really true that more than a million has been subscribed?"
"Yes, princess."
"What do you make of today's telegram? The Turks beaten again."

"Yes, I saw it," Sergey Ivanovitch answered. They were referring to the latest telegram saying that the Turks had been beaten at every point for three days running and put to flight, and that a decisive engagement was expected the next day.

"Oh, by the way, a fine young man has asked for leave to go, and they've made some kind of difficulty about it, I don't know why. I was going to ask you — I know him; please write a note on his behalf. He's being sent by Countess Lidia Ivanovna."

Sergey Ivanovitch got all the details the princess knew about the young man, and going into the first-class waiting room, wrote a note to the person who could grant the leave and handed it to the princess.
"You know Count Vronsky, the notorious one ... is taking this train?" the princess said with a smile full of triumph and meaning, when he found her again and gave her the letter.
"I had heard he was going, but I didn't know when. By this train?"
"I've seen him. He's here — only his mother is seeing him off. It's the best thing he could do, really."
"Yes, of course."

While they were talking, the crowd streamed past them into the dining room. They moved forward too, and heard a gentleman with a glass in his hand giving a loud speech to the volunteers. "In the service of religion, humanity, and our brothers," the gentleman was saying, his voice rising louder and louder; "to this great cause Mother Moscow dedicates you with her blessing. _Jivio!_" he ended, in a loud, tearful tone.
Everyone shouted _Jivio!_ and a fresh wave of people dashed into the hall, nearly knocking the princess off her feet.

"Ah, princess! That was really something!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, suddenly turning up in the middle of the crowd and beaming at them with a delighted smile. "Splendidly, warmly put, wasn't it? Bravo! And Sergey Ivanovitch! Really, you should have said something too — just a few words, you know, to encourage them; you do that so well," he added with a soft, deferential, discreet smile, gently nudging Sergey Ivanovitch forward by the arm.
"No, I'm just leaving."
"Where to?"
"To the country, to my brother's," Sergey Ivanovitch answered.

"Then you'll see my wife. I've written to her, but you'll see her before the letter does. Please tell her that they've seen me, and that it's 'all right,' as the English say. She'll understand. Oh, and be kind enough to tell her I've been appointed secretary of the committee.... But she'll understand! You know, _les petites misères de la vie humaine_," he said, as if apologizing to the princess. "And Princess Myakaya — not Liza, but Bibish — is sending a thousand guns and twelve nurses. Did I tell you?"
"Yes, I'd heard," Koznishev answered, indifferent.

"It's a pity you're leaving," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "Tomorrow we're giving a dinner for two who are setting off — Dimer-Bartnyansky from Petersburg and our own Veslovsky, Grisha. They're both going. Veslovsky's only just got married. What a man, eh? Eh, princess?" he said, turning to the lady.

The princess looked at Koznishev without answering. But the fact that Sergey Ivanovitch and the princess seemed eager to get rid of him did not faze Stepan Arkadyevitch in the slightest. Smiling, he stared at the feather in the princess's hat and then around him as though he were about to spot something to pick up. Catching sight of a lady approaching with a collecting box, he waved her over and dropped in a five-rouble note.
"I can never look at one of these collecting boxes unmoved as long as I've got money in my pocket," he said. "And what about today's telegram? Splendid lads, those Montenegrins!"

"You don't say!" he cried, when the princess told him Vronsky was taking this train. For a moment Stepan Arkadyevitch's face turned sad, but a minute later, when, stroking his mustaches and swaying as he walked, he went into the hall where Vronsky was, he had completely forgotten his own desperate sobs over his sister's body, and saw in Vronsky only a hero and an old friend.

"With all his faults, you can't deny the man his due," the princess said to Sergey Ivanovitch as soon as Stepan Arkadyevitch had left them. "What a thoroughly Russian, Slavic nature! Only, I'm afraid it won't be pleasant for Vronsky to see him. Say what you will, I'm touched by that man's fate. Do talk to him a little along the way," the princess said.
"Yes, perhaps, if it works out that way."
"I never liked him. But this makes up for a great deal. He's not just going himself — he's taking a whole squadron at his own expense."
"Yes, so I'd heard."

A bell rang. Everyone crowded toward the doors. "There he is!" said the princess, pointing to Vronsky, who walked past with his mother on his arm, wearing a long overcoat and a wide-brimmed black hat. Oblonsky was walking beside him, talking eagerly about something.
Vronsky was frowning and looking straight ahead, as if he wasn't hearing what Stepan Arkadyevitch was saying.

Probably because Oblonsky pointed them out, he looked over toward where the princess and Sergey Ivanovitch were standing, and without speaking lifted his hat. His face, aged and worn by suffering, looked like stone.
Going out onto the platform, Vronsky left his mother and disappeared into a compartment.

On the platform "God save the Tsar" rang out, then shouts of "hurrah!" and _"jivio!"_ One of the volunteers, a tall young man with a hollow chest, was particularly conspicuous, bowing and waving his felt hat and a nosegay above his head. Then two officers came out, bowing too, and a stout man with a big beard, in a greasy forage cap.

title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: After saying goodbye to the princess, Sergey Ivanovitch was joined by Katavasov; they squeezed into a carriage that was already packed, and the train pulled out.

At Tsaritsino station a chorus of young men met the train, singing "Hail to Thee!" Once more the volunteers bowed and craned their heads out the windows, but Sergey Ivanovitch took no notice. He had dealt with so many volunteers by now that the type was familiar to him and held no interest. Katavasov, whose scientific work had kept him from observing them up to now, was fascinated by them and started asking Sergey Ivanovitch questions.
Sergey Ivanovitch suggested he move into second-class and talk to the volunteers himself. At the next station, Katavasov did exactly that.

At the first stop he shifted into second-class and made the acquaintance of the volunteers. They had settled into a corner of the carriage, talking loudly and plainly conscious that the other passengers — and Katavasov, as he came in — were all watching them. The loudest of them was a tall, hollow-chested young man. He was clearly tipsy, and was telling some story from his school days. Across from him sat a middle-aged officer in the Austrian-style jacket of the Guards uniform. He was listening to the hollow-chested youth with a smile, now and then pulling him back into line. The third, in artillery uniform, was perched on a box beside them. A fourth was asleep.

Once Katavasov got the young man talking, he found out he was a wealthy Moscow merchant who had blown through a sizable fortune before he turned twenty-two. Katavasov took an instant dislike to him: he struck him as unmanly, soft, and unhealthy. The young man was clearly convinced, especially now that he had been drinking, that he was performing some heroic act, and he bragged about it in the most off-putting way.

The second man, the retired officer, also gave Katavasov a bad impression. He seemed to be the kind of person who had tried his hand at everything. He had worked on a railway, been a land steward, started factories, and he kept bringing it all up with no real reason, dropping technical terms in places where they didn't fit.

The third one, the artilleryman, struck Katavasov very differently — favorably. He was quiet and modest, plainly impressed by the officer's expertise and the merchant's heroic self-sacrifice, and he said nothing about himself. When Katavasov asked him what had pushed him to go to Servia, he answered with a shrug:
"Well, everyone's going. The Servians need help too. I feel sorry for them."
"Yes, artillerymen especially are in short supply over there," Katavasov said.
"Oh, I wasn't in the artillery for long. Maybe they'll put me in the infantry or the cavalry."
"The infantry? When they need artillery more than anything?" said Katavasov, guessing from the artilleryman's apparent age that he must have reached a fairly senior rank.
"I wasn't long in the artillery — I'm a cadet, retired," he said, and he started explaining how he had failed his examination.

Taken together, all of this left a bad taste in Katavasov's mouth, and when the volunteers stepped off at a station for a drink, he was eager to compare notes with someone. There was an old man in the carriage, in a military overcoat, who had been listening the whole time to Katavasov's conversation with the volunteers. Once they were alone, Katavasov turned to him.
"Quite a mix of backgrounds, those men going off to Servia," Katavasov said vaguely, not wanting to show his own hand yet, while trying to draw out the old man's opinion.

The old man was an officer who had served in two campaigns. He knew what made a real soldier, and going by the look of these volunteers and the way they talked — by the swagger with which they had reached for the bottle on the trip — he judged them to be poor material. On top of that, he lived in a district town, and he was itching to mention how one volunteer from his town had been a drunk and a thief no one would even take on as a laborer. But he knew from experience that in the current public mood it was dangerous to voice an opinion that went against the crowd, especially anything critical of the volunteers, so he too kept watching Katavasov without committing to anything.

"Well, they need men over there," he said, his eyes laughing. And the two of them slipped into discussing the latest war news, each hiding from the other his confusion about the battle expected the next day, since according to the latest reports the Turks had been beaten on every front. So they parted, neither one of them having said what he really thought.
Back in his own carriage, Katavasov, swallowing his honesty, gave Sergey Ivanovitch an edited account of what he had seen of the volunteers — one in which they came out sounding like first-rate men.

At a large station in a town, the volunteers were greeted again with shouts and singing, again with men and women holding collection boxes and provincial ladies bringing bouquets and following them into the refreshment room — but all of it on a much smaller, weaker scale than in Moscow.

title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: While the train was stopped at the provincial town, Sergey Ivanovitch did not head to the refreshment room — he walked up and down the platform instead.
The first time he passed Vronsky's compartment, he noticed the curtain was drawn over the window. The second time he passed, he saw the old countess at the window. She waved him over.
"I'm going along, as you can see — taking him as far as Kursk," she said.
"Yes, I heard," said Sergey Ivanovitch, stopping by her window and looking in. "What a noble thing for him to do," he added, when he noticed Vronsky wasn't in the compartment.
"After what happened to him, what else was there for him to do?"
"What a terrible thing," said Sergey Ivanovitch.

"Ah, what I've been through! But come in — please. Ah, what I've been through!" she said again, once Sergey Ivanovitch had stepped inside and taken a seat beside her. "You can't imagine. For six weeks he didn't speak to anyone, and he wouldn't touch food unless I begged him to. And we couldn't leave him alone for a single minute. We took away anything he could have used on himself. We were on the ground floor, but there was no being sure of anything. You know, of course, that he had already shot himself once over her," she said, and the old lady's eyelashes twitched at the memory. "Yes — hers was a fitting end for a woman like that. Even the death she chose was low and vulgar."
"It isn't for us to judge, Countess," said Sergey Ivanovitch. "But I can well understand how hard this has been for you."

"Ah, don't make me talk about it! I was at my estate, and he was there with me. A note was brought to him. He wrote an answer and sent it off. We had no idea she was right there at the station. In the evening, I had only just gone to my room when my Mary came in and told me a lady had thrown herself under the train. Something inside me knew right away. I knew it was her. The first thing I said was — he must not be told. But they'd already told him. His coachman was there and saw the whole thing. When I ran into his room, he was beside himself — it was terrible to see. He didn't say a single word — he just galloped off to the spot. To this day I don't know what went on there, but they brought him back at death's door. I would not have known him. _Prostration complète_, the doctor called it. And it was followed almost immediately by something close to madness. Oh, why bring it up," the countess said, waving her hand. "It was a dreadful time! No — say what you will, she was a bad woman. What is the point of such reckless passions? It was all just to make herself something out of the ordinary. Well, she certainly managed that. She destroyed herself and two good men along with her — her husband and my unhappy son."
"And what did her husband do?" Sergey Ivanovitch asked.

"He's taken her little girl. At first Alexey was ready to agree to anything. Now it eats at him, that he handed his own child over to another man. But he can't take his word back. Karenin came to the funeral. We did try to keep him from meeting Alexey. For him — for her husband — it was easier, anyway. She had set him free. But my poor son had given himself over completely to her. He had thrown away everything — his career, me — and even then she had no pity on him; she ruined him on purpose, all the way down. No — say what you will, the very way she died was the death of a vile woman, with no faith in her. God forgive me, but I can't help hating her memory when I look at how miserable my son is."
"And how is he now?"

"This Servian war has been a blessing from heaven for us. I'm old, and I don't understand the rights and wrongs of it, but for him it's come as a providential blessing. Of course as his mother it's awful for me, and what makes it worse — they say _ce n'est pas très bien vu à Pétersbourg_. But what can be done? It was the one thing that could wake him up. Yashvin — a friend of his — had lost everything at cards and was going to Servia. He came to see him and talked him into going. Now he has something to occupy him. Please, do talk to him a little. I want to take his mind off things. He's so low. And as ill luck would have it, he has toothache on top of everything. But he'll be glad to see you. Please, talk to him — he's pacing on that side over there."
Sergey Ivanovitch said he would be very glad to, and crossed over to the other side of the station.

title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: In the slanting evening shadows thrown by the luggage piled up on the platform, Vronsky — in his long overcoat and slouch hat, hands in his pockets — paced up and down like a caged animal, turning sharply every twenty paces. As Sergey Ivanovitch came toward him, he had the impression Vronsky had seen him but was pretending not to. It made no difference at all to Sergey Ivanovitch. He had risen above any personal feeling about Vronsky.

At that moment Sergey Ivanovitch regarded Vronsky as a man taking on an important role in a great cause, and Koznishev felt it was his duty to encourage him and let him know he approved. He walked up to him.
Vronsky stopped, looked at him hard, recognized him, and stepped a few paces forward to meet him, shaking his hand warmly.
"You may not have wanted to see me," said Sergey Ivanovitch, "but couldn't I be useful to you in some way?"
"There's no one I'd less mind seeing than you," Vronsky said. "Forgive me — there's nothing in life left that I do want."

"I understand completely. I only meant to offer my help," said Sergey Ivanovitch, studying Vronsky's face, which carried unmistakable signs of suffering. "Would a letter to Ristitch — to Milan — be useful?"

"Oh, no!" said Vronsky, as if he were having trouble following. "If you don't mind, let's keep walking. It's too stuffy near the carriages. A letter? No, thank you — you don't need a letter of introduction to go meet death. And not for the Turks either —" he said, with a smile that was only on his lips. His eyes kept their look of angry pain.

"Yes — but a connection like that might make it easier to get in touch with the people you'll need to work with. Still, suit yourself. I was very glad to hear what you intend to do. The volunteers have been attacked from every side, and a man like you raises the whole effort in the public's eyes."

"My value as a man," Vronsky said, "is that my life is worth nothing to me. And that I still have enough physical strength to cut my way into their ranks and either trample them or fall. That much I know. I'm glad there's something I can spend my life on, since to me it isn't just useless, it's hateful. Anyone is welcome to it." And his jaw twitched impatiently from the steady gnawing of his toothache, which kept him from even speaking with his normal expression.

"You'll become another man — I'm sure of it," Sergey Ivanovitch said, moved. "To deliver your fellow men from slavery is an aim worth dying and living for. May God grant you outward success — and inward peace," he added, and held out his hand. Vronsky pressed it warmly.
"Yes — as a weapon I may still be of some use. But as a man, I'm finished," he forced out.

He could barely speak through the throbbing in his strong teeth, which sat in his mouth like rows of ivory. He was silent, his eyes fixed on the wheels of the tender as they rolled smoothly along the rails.

And suddenly a different pain — not a physical ache but an inner anguish that gripped his whole being — made him forget the toothache for an instant. As he looked at the tender and the rails, with the conversation he had just had with someone he hadn't seen since his disaster, he remembered _her_ — that is, what was left of her when he had run, half out of his mind, into the cloakroom of the railway station — sprawled shamelessly on the table among strangers, the blood-stained body that had been so full of life only a moment before; the head untouched, falling back under the weight of its hair, the curls at the temples, the exquisite face, the half-open red mouth, the strange fixed expression — pitiful on the lips and terrible in the still-open eyes — that seemed to be repeating that awful phrase she had said when they were fighting: that he would be sorry for this.

He tried to picture her the way she had been when they first met, also at a railway station — mysterious, lovely, in love, seeking happiness and giving it, not cruelly vengeful the way he remembered her at the end. He tried to call up his best moments with her, but those moments were poisoned forever. The only image he could hold was of her triumphant — having made good on her threat to lay on him a remorse that could never be cleared. He stopped feeling the toothache; his face was working with sobs.
After walking past the baggage twice more in silence and getting hold of himself, he turned back to Sergey Ivanovitch and spoke calmly:
"Have you had any telegrams since yesterday's? Yes — driven back for a third time, but a decisive engagement is expected for tomorrow."
They talked a little more about King Milan's proclamation and the huge impact it could have, then parted as the second bell rang, each heading to his own carriage.

title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: Sergey Ivanovitch had not wired ahead to his brother to send someone to meet him, since he hadn't known when he would manage to get out of Moscow. Levin was not at home when Katavasov and Sergey Ivanovitch — in a fly they had hired at the station — pulled up to the steps of the house at Pokrovskoe, as black as Moors from the dust of the road. Kitty, who was sitting on the balcony with her father and sister, recognized her brother-in-law and ran down to meet him.
"What a shame you didn't let us know," she said, giving Sergey Ivanovitch her hand and lifting her forehead for a kiss.

"We had a fine drive, and we haven't put you to any trouble," Sergey Ivanovitch said. "I'm so filthy, I'm afraid to touch you. I've been so busy I didn't know when I could break away. And so you're still the same as ever, enjoying your peaceful, quiet happiness," he said, smiling, "out of the way of the current, in your peaceful backwater. And here's our friend Fyodor Vassilievitch, who has finally managed to come along too."
"But I'm no negro — I'll look like a human being once I wash," said Katavasov in his usual joking tone, and he shook hands and smiled, his teeth flashing white against his blackened face.
"Kostya will be thrilled. He's gone over to his settlement. He ought to be home any moment."

"Still buried in his farming. It really is a peaceful backwater," said Katavasov. "Meanwhile, in town we can't think about anything except the Servian war. So — what's our friend's take on it? He's never one to think like everyone else."

"Oh, I don't really know — much like everyone, I think," Kitty answered, a little flustered, glancing over at Sergey Ivanovitch. "I'll send someone to fetch him. Papa is staying with us. He's only just come back from abroad."

And after seeing to it that someone went after Levin, and that the guests had what they needed to wash up — one in his own room, the other in what used to be Dolly's — and ordering lunch, Kitty ran back out onto the balcony, enjoying the freedom and quickness of her movements after months of being slowed down by pregnancy.
"It's Sergey Ivanovitch, and Katavasov, a professor," she said.
"Oh — that's a nuisance in this heat," said the prince.
"No, papa, he's very pleasant, and Kostya is very fond of him," Kitty said, with an apologetic smile, catching the ironic look on her father's face.
"Oh, I didn't say anything."

"You go to them, darling," Kitty said to her sister, "and entertain them. They saw Stiva at the station — he was quite well. And I need to run to Mitya. As bad luck would have it, I haven't fed him since tea. He's awake now and he's sure to be screaming." And feeling her milk come in, she hurried to the nursery.
It wasn't just a guess. Her bond with the baby was still so close that she could tell from the rush of her milk that he needed feeding, and she knew for sure he was hungry.

She could hear him crying before she reached the nursery. And sure enough he was. She heard him and walked faster. But the faster she went, the louder he screamed. It was a fine healthy scream — hungry and impatient.

"Has he been crying long, nurse, very long?" Kitty asked hurriedly, dropping into a chair and getting ready to give the baby the breast. "Just give him to me — quickly. Oh, nurse, you are such a bother! Tie the cap afterwards, please!"
The baby's greedy scream was turning into sobs.
"But you can't do it that way, ma'am," said Agafea Mihalovna, who was almost always to be found in the nursery. "He has to be set straight. A-oo! a-oo!" she crooned over him, ignoring the mother.
The nurse brought the baby to his mother. Agafea Mihalovna followed them with a face melting with tenderness.
"He knows me, he knows me! God's truth, Katerina Alexandrovna, ma'am, he knew me!" Agafea Mihalovna called out over the baby's screams.
But Kitty wasn't listening to her. Her impatience was rising, just like the baby's.
Their impatience held things up for a little while. The baby couldn't latch on properly and was furious.
Finally, after desperate, breathless screaming and a lot of useless sucking, things sorted themselves out, and mother and child relaxed at the same moment and both settled into calm.
"Poor little darling — he's drenched in sweat!" Kitty whispered, touching the baby.

"What makes you think he knows you?" she added, with a sideways glance at the baby's eyes — which seemed to her to peek out roguishly from under his cap — and at his rhythmically pumping cheeks, and the little hand with its red palm that he kept waving around.
"Impossible! If he knew anybody, he'd know me first," Kitty said in response to Agafea Mihalovna's claim, and she smiled.

She smiled because, even though she had said he couldn't possibly know her, in her heart she was sure he knew not only Agafea Mihalovna — he knew and understood everything, including a great deal that nobody else knew, things she herself, his mother, had only learned and come to understand because of him. For Agafea Mihalovna, for the nurse, for his grandfather, even for his father, Mitya was a living creature who needed nothing but physical care; but for his mother he had long been a moral being, with whom a whole series of inward exchanges had already taken place.
"When he wakes up, please God, you'll see for yourself. When I do like this, he simply beams at me, the darling! Beams like a sunny day!" said Agafea Mihalovna.
"All right, all right — we'll see," Kitty whispered. "But now go away — he's about to fall asleep."

title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Agafea Mihalovna stepped out on tiptoe. The nurse let down the blind, chased a fly out from under the muslin canopy of the crib and a bumblebee that had been struggling against the window-frame, and sat down, fanning a faded birch branch over the mother and the baby.
"How hot it is. If only God would send a bit of rain," she said.

"Yes, yes, sh — sh — sh —" was all Kitty answered, rocking gently and tenderly squeezing the plump little arm with its rolls of fat at the wrist that Mitya was still waving weakly as he opened and closed his eyes. That hand kept tugging at Kitty; she longed to kiss it but was afraid she would wake him. Finally the little hand stopped waving and the eyes closed. From time to time, as he kept sucking, the baby raised his long, curly eyelashes and peeked at his mother with wet eyes that looked black in the twilight. The nurse had stopped fanning and was dozing off. From upstairs came the booming of the old prince's voice and Katavasov's chuckle.

"They've started talking without me," Kitty thought. "It is annoying that Kostya is out, though. He's probably back at the bee-house again. It's a pity he's there so often, but I'm glad of it. It takes his mind off things. He's so much happier and steadier now than he was in the spring. Back then he was so gloomy and tense I was frightened for him. And how funny he is!" she whispered, smiling.

She knew what was bothering her husband. It was his lack of faith. Even though, if anyone had asked her whether she believed that in the next life an unbeliever would be damned, she would have had to admit he would be, his unbelief did not make her unhappy. And while she accepted that for an unbeliever there could be no salvation, and loved her husband's soul more than anything in the world, she could still smile at his unbelief and tell herself he was simply absurd.

"What's the point of him reading philosophy of some kind all year long?" she wondered. "If everything's in those books, then he can understand them. If it's all wrong, why does he read them? He says himself that he would like to believe. So why doesn't he? Surely from thinking so much about it. And he thinks so much because he's so alone. He's always by himself. He can't talk about any of this with us. I think he'll be glad to have these visitors — especially Katavasov. He enjoys debates with them," she thought, and her mind jumped at once to the question of where it would be best to put Katavasov: in a room by himself, or sharing Sergey Ivanovitch's. Then an idea suddenly hit her that made her flinch hard enough to disturb Mitya, who shot her a stern look. "I'm sure the laundress hasn't sent the washing back yet, and all the best sheets are out. If I don't see to it, Agafea Mihalovna will give Sergey Ivanovitch the wrong sheets." At the very thought, the blood rushed into Kitty's face.

"Yes — I'll arrange it," she decided, and going back to her earlier train of thought, she remembered that some important spiritual question had been broken off, and she tried to recover what it was. "Yes — Kostya, the unbeliever," she thought again, smiling.
"All right, an unbeliever then! Better that than to be like Madame Stahl, or like what I tried to be back in those days abroad. No — he'll never put on an act about anything."

And a recent example of his goodness came vividly to mind. Two weeks earlier, a remorseful letter had arrived from Stepan Arkadyevitch to Dolly. He begged her to save his honor — to sell her estate to cover his debts. Dolly was in despair. She loathed her husband, despised him, pitied him, decided on a separation, decided to refuse, but in the end agreed to sell part of her property. After that — with a tender smile she couldn't hold back — Kitty remembered her husband's embarrassed awkwardness, his repeated clumsy attempts to bring up the subject, and how at last, having thought of the one way to help Dolly without bruising her pride, he had suggested to Kitty something that hadn't occurred to her before: that she should give up her own share of the property.

"He, an unbeliever — really! With that heart of his, that fear of hurting anyone, even a child! Everything for others, nothing for himself. Sergey Ivanovitch just takes it as Kostya's job to act as his steward. It's the same with his sister. Now Dolly and her children are under his protection — and all those peasants who come to him every day, as if he were obliged to be at their service."
"Yes — only be like your father, just like him," she said, handing Mitya back to the nurse and pressing her lips to his cheek.

title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Ever since Levin had first looked into the questions of life and death by his beloved brother's deathbed — in the light of what he called these new convictions, which between the ages of twenty and thirty-four had quietly taken the place of his boyhood and youthful beliefs — he had been gripped by a horror, not so much of death as of life: a life with no knowledge of where it came from, why, how, or what it was. The physical organism, its decay, the indestructibility of matter, the law of conservation of energy, evolution — these were the words that had pushed his old faith out of the way. The words and the ideas attached to them were perfectly serviceable for intellectual work. But for life itself they offered nothing, and Levin felt suddenly like a man who has traded a warm fur cloak for a thin muslin shirt and, going out into the frost for the first time, is convinced — not by reasoning but by his whole body — that he is as good as naked and certain to perish horribly.
From that moment on, even though he didn't put it to himself directly and went on living as he always had, Levin had never lost that sense of terror at how little he knew.

He also dimly felt that what he called his new convictions weren't merely a gap in his knowledge — they were part of a whole framework of ideas inside which the knowledge he needed simply wasn't available.

At first, marriage, with all the new joys and responsibilities that came with it, had crowded these thoughts out completely. But lately — while he was staying in Moscow after his wife's confinement, with nothing in particular to do — the question that demanded an answer had been pressing on him more and more often, more and more insistently.

He boiled it down to this: "If I don't accept the answers Christianity gives to the basic problems of my life, what answers do I accept?" And in the whole stockpile of his convictions, not only did he find no satisfying answer — he could find nothing that even resembled an answer.
He was in the position of a man hunting for food in toy shops and tool shops.
Instinctively, almost unconsciously, with every book, every conversation, every person he came across, he was scanning for some light on these questions and a way out of them.

What baffled and unsettled him most was that the majority of the men of his age and class had, like him, swapped their old beliefs for the same new convictions, and yet saw nothing to regret in it — they were perfectly satisfied and at ease. So beyond the central question, Levin was tormented by other questions too. Were these people sincere? he asked himself. Or were they putting on an act? Or did they understand the answers science offered to these problems in some other, clearer way than he did? And he diligently studied both their views and the books that laid out those scientific explanations.

One thing he had figured out since these questions had taken hold of him was that he had been quite wrong in thinking — based on memories of his college circle — that religion had had its day and was now practically gone. All the people closest to him who lived good lives were believers. The old prince, and Lvov, whom he liked so much, and Sergey Ivanovitch, and all the women believed; his wife believed as simply as he had believed in his earliest childhood; and ninety-nine hundredths of the Russian people — all the working people whose lives he had the deepest respect for — believed.

Another thing he had become sure of, after reading many scientific books, was that the men who shared his views had no other interpretation to offer — they gave no explanation of the questions he felt he could not live without answering, but simply ignored that those questions existed and tried instead to explain other questions he had no interest in, such as the evolution of organisms, the materialist theory of consciousness, and so on.

On top of that, during his wife's confinement, something had happened that struck him as extraordinary. He, an unbeliever, had found himself praying, and in the moment of prayer he had believed. But that moment had passed, and he couldn't make the state of mind he had been in then fit into the rest of his life.

He couldn't admit that in that moment he had known the truth and was now wrong, because as soon as he started thinking about it calmly, the whole thing fell apart. He couldn't admit that he had been mistaken back then either, because that spiritual condition was precious to him, and to call it a sign of weakness would have been to defile those moments. He was painfully at war with himself, and he was straining every spiritual muscle to find a way out of the situation.

title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: These doubts gnawed at him and wore him down, easing or sharpening from time to time but never leaving him. He read and he thought, and the more he read and the more he thought, the further he felt from the goal he was chasing.

Lately in Moscow and out in the country — once he had become convinced he would find no solution in the materialists — he had read and re-read carefully Plato, Spinoza, Kant, Schelling, Hegel, and Schopenhauer, the philosophers who offered a non-materialist account of life.

Their ideas seemed fruitful to him when he was reading them, or when he was looking for arguments against rival theories, especially the materialist ones; but as soon as he turned to find a solution to the problems for himself, the same thing always happened. As long as he stuck to the fixed definitions of obscure words like _spirit, will, freedom, essence_, deliberately letting himself fall into the verbal traps the philosophers laid for him, he seemed to be understanding something. But the moment he stepped away from the artificial chain of reasoning and turned from life itself back to what had satisfied him while he was thinking by the rules of those definitions, the whole artificial structure fell apart at once like a house of cards, and it became clear that the structure had been built up out of those rearranged words, with nothing more important than reason to hold it together.

At one point, while he was reading Schopenhauer, he tried substituting the word _love_ for _will_, and for a couple of days this new philosophy enchanted him — until he stepped a little away from it. But then, when he turned from life back to look at it again, it crumbled too, and turned out to be the same muslin shirt that gave no warmth at all.

His brother Sergey Ivanovitch advised him to read the theological works of Homiakov. Levin read the second volume of Homiakov's writings and, despite the polished, epigrammatic, argumentative style that put him off at first, he was struck by the doctrine of the church he found there. He was struck above all by the idea that the grasp of divine truths had not been granted to any single man but to a body of men bound together by love — to the church. What delighted him was the thought of how much easier it was to believe in a living, still-existing church, which contained all the beliefs of mankind and had God at its head and was therefore holy and infallible, and to receive from that church the faith in God, in creation, the fall, redemption — rather than to start with God, a mysterious, distant God, then creation, and so on. But afterwards, when he read a Catholic writer's history of the church and then a Greek Orthodox writer's history of the church, and saw that the two churches, each defined as infallible, each denied the authority of the other, Homiakov's doctrine of the church lost all its appeal for him, and this structure crumbled into dust the way the philosophers' structures had.
All that spring he was not himself, and he went through terrifying stretches of dread.
"Without knowing what I am and why I'm here, life is impossible — and I can't know, so I can't live," Levin told himself.
"Inside endless time, endless matter, endless space, a little bubble-organism takes shape; the bubble holds for a while, and then it pops — and that bubble is Me."
It was an excruciating error, but it was the only logical outcome of centuries of human thought running in that direction.

This was the ultimate belief on which almost every system human thought had ever constructed, in almost all its branches, rested. It was the prevailing conviction, and out of all the available explanations Levin had unconsciously — without knowing when or how — picked this one as the clearest and made it his own.
But it wasn't merely a lie — it was the cruel mockery of some malicious power, some evil, hateful power that one could not submit to.
He had to escape from that power. And every man had the means of escape in his own hands. He only had to cut short this dependence on evil. And there was one way out — death.

And Levin, a happy father and husband, in perfect health, came so close to suicide several times that he hid the cord so he wouldn't be tempted to hang himself, and was afraid to go out with his gun in case he shot himself.
But Levin did not shoot himself, and did not hang himself. He went on living.

title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: When Levin thought about what he was and what he was living for, he could find no answer to the questions and was reduced to despair — so he stopped asking himself. It was as though he did know what he was and what he was living for, since he acted and lived with resolve and without hesitation. In fact, in those days he was more decisive and surer in life than he had ever been.

When he went back to the country at the beginning of June, he also went back to his usual occupations. Running the estate, his dealings with the peasants and the neighbors, the management of his household, looking after his sister's and brother's properties — which he was in charge of — his relationships with his wife and her family, the care of his child, and the new beekeeping hobby he had picked up that spring all filled up his time.

These things absorbed him now, not because he could justify them to himself by some set of general principles, the way he used to. On the contrary, disillusioned by the failure of his earlier efforts for the common good, and too occupied with his own thoughts and the pile of business pressing on him from every direction, he had given up entirely on thinking about the general welfare. He went about all this work simply because it seemed to him that he had to do it — that he could not do otherwise. In the old days — practically from childhood, and increasingly into full manhood — whenever he had tried to do something that would be good for all, for humanity, for Russia, for the whole village, he had noticed that the idea of it was pleasant, but the work itself was always confused, that he was never fully convinced it was strictly necessary, and that the project, which had begun by looking so grand, would shrink smaller and smaller until it vanished into nothing. But now, since his marriage, when he had begun to confine himself more and more to living for himself, even though he felt no particular pleasure at the thought of the work he was doing, he felt a total conviction that it was necessary, saw that it succeeded far better than in earlier days, and that it kept growing.
Now, almost against his own will, he was cutting deeper and deeper into the soil like a plough, so that he could not be pulled back out without turning the furrow aside.

To live the same kind of family life his father and forefathers had lived — that is, on the same cultural footing — and to bring up his children in the same way, was unquestionably necessary. It was as necessary as eating when you were hungry. And to do that, just as it was necessary to cook a meal, it was necessary to keep the machinery of farming at Pokrovskoe running so that it produced an income. Just as unmistakably as it was necessary to repay a debt, it was necessary to keep the estate in such shape that his son, when he received it, would say "thank you" to his father, the same way Levin had said "thank you" to his grandfather for everything he had built and planted. And to do that, it was necessary to look after the land himself, not lease it out, and to breed cattle, fertilize the fields, and plant trees.

It was impossible not to look after Sergey Ivanovitch's affairs, his sister's, and the peasants' who came to him for advice and were used to doing so — as impossible as dropping a child you're carrying in your arms. It was necessary to see to the comfort of his sister-in-law and her children, and of his wife and the baby, and impossible not to spend at least a small part of each day with them.
All of this, together with shooting and the new beekeeping, filled up the whole of Levin's life — a life that had no meaning at all for him as soon as he began to think.
But besides knowing thoroughly what he had to do, Levin also knew, in just the same way, _how_ he had to do all of it, and which things mattered more than the rest.

He knew he had to hire workers as cheaply as he could, but to hire men under bond — paying them up front at less than the going wage — was something he must not do, however profitable it would have been. Selling straw to the peasants when feed was scarce was something he could do, even though he felt sorry for them; but the tavern and the pothouse had to be shut down, even though they brought in income. Cutting down his timber had to be punished as severely as possible, but he couldn't impose fines on peasants whose cattle wandered into his fields; and though it annoyed the gamekeeper and made the peasants unafraid to graze their cattle on his land, he couldn't impound their animals as a penalty.

He had to lend Pyotr, who was paying a money-lender ten per cent a month, enough to get clear of him. But he couldn't let peasants who didn't pay their rent off the hook, or let them fall into arrears. There was no overlooking the bailiff's failure to mow the meadows and letting the hay rot — and equally, no way to mow the acres where a young copse had been planted. There was no excusing a laborer who had gone home in the busy season because his father was dying, however much sympathy he had for him, and he had to dock those expensive idle months from his pay. But there was no question of refusing the monthly rations to the old servants who weren't fit for anything else.

Levin knew that when he got home he would have to go first to his wife, who wasn't well, and that the peasants who had been waiting three hours to see him could wait a little longer. He also knew that, however much pleasure he got out of taking a swarm, he would have to give up that pleasure and leave the old man to handle the bees alone, while he talked to the peasants who had followed him out to the bee-house.
Whether he was doing the right thing or the wrong thing he did not know, and far from trying to prove that he was right, these days he avoided any thought or talk about it.

Reasoning had led him to doubt, and stopped him from seeing what he ought to do and what he ought not. When he didn't think, but simply lived, he was constantly aware of an infallible judge in his soul deciding which of two possible courses of action was the better and which was the worse, and the moment he didn't act rightly, he knew it.

So he lived, not knowing and not seeing any way of finding out what he was or what he was living for, and tormented by that ignorance to such a degree that he was afraid of suicide — and yet steadily laying down his own particular, definite path in life.

title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: The day Sergey Ivanovitch arrived at Pokrovskoe was one of Levin's most painful days. It was the busiest stretch of the working season, when the whole peasantry shows an extraordinary intensity of self-sacrificing labor — the kind that's never shown under any other conditions, and would be highly admired if the men who showed it admired it in themselves, if it didn't happen every year, and if the results of all this intense work weren't so plain.

To reap and bind the rye and oats and haul them in, to mow the meadows, turn over the fallows, thresh the seed and sow the winter corn — all of it sounds so simple and ordinary. But to get through it all, everyone in the village, from the old man down to the small child, has to work flat out for three or four weeks — three times as hard as usual — living on rye-beer, onions, and black bread, threshing and carrying the sheaves through the night, and sleeping no more than two or three hours out of twenty-four. And every year this is done all over Russia.
Having spent most of his life in the country and in close contact with the peasants, Levin always felt at this busy time of year that he caught the general surge of energy running through the people.

Early in the morning he rode out to where the first rye was being sown, and to the oats, which were being carted to the stacks. Coming back by the time his wife and sister-in-law were getting up, he had coffee with them and walked over to the farm, where a new threshing machine was about to be set up to prepare the seed-corn.

He was standing in the cool granary, still fragrant with the leaves of the hazel branches woven into the freshly stripped aspen beams of the new thatched roof. He looked through the open door, where the dry, bitter dust of threshing whirled and danced, at the grass of the threshing floor in the sunlight and the fresh straw that had just been brought in from the barn, then at the speckle-headed, white-breasted swallows that flew chirping in under the roof and, fluttering their wings, settled in the cracks of the doorway, then at the peasants bustling around in the dark, dusty barn — and as he watched, strange thoughts came to him.

"Why is all of this being done?" he thought. "Why am I standing here, making them work? What are they all so busy for, trying to show how hard they're working in front of me? What is old Matrona, my old friend, working herself like this for? (I treated her after the beam fell on her in the fire,)" he thought, looking at a thin old woman raking up the grain, moving painfully on bare, sun-blackened feet across the rough, uneven floor. "She recovered then — but today or tomorrow or in ten years, she won't; they'll bury her, and nothing will be left, of her or of that smart girl in the red jacket who's shaking the grain out of the husks with such a skillful, easy motion. They'll bury her too — and that piebald horse, and pretty soon," he thought, looking at the heavily moving, panting horse that kept tramping up the wheel turning underneath him. "And they'll bury her, and Fyodor the thresher, with his curly beard full of chaff and his shirt torn over his white shoulders — they'll bury him too. He's untying the sheaves and giving orders and shouting at the women and quickly straightening the strap on the moving wheel. And what's more, it isn't just them — they'll bury me as well, and nothing will be left. What for?"
He thought all of this and at the same time looked at his watch to figure out how much they were threshing in an hour. He needed to know in order to judge the day's quota.

"It's almost one, and they're only beginning the third sheaf," Levin thought. He walked up to the man who was feeding the machine, and shouting over the roar of it told him to put it in more slowly. "You're feeding in too much at once, Fyodor. See — it gets choked, that's why it isn't moving. Do it evenly."
Fyodor, black with the dust that stuck to his sweating face, shouted something back, but went on doing it the way Levin didn't want him to.

Levin walked up to the machine, edged Fyodor out of the way, and started feeding the corn in himself. He kept working until the peasants' dinner hour, which came soon enough, then walked out of the barn with Fyodor and fell into conversation with him, stopping beside a neat yellow sheaf of rye laid out on the threshing floor for seed.

Fyodor came from a village some distance away from the one where Levin had once granted land to his cooperative association. The land in that other village had now been leased to a former house porter.
Levin asked Fyodor about that land, and whether Platon, a well-off peasant of good character from the same village, would take it on for the coming year.
"The rent's too high — it wouldn't pay for Platon, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," the peasant answered, picking ears of grain off his sweat-soaked shirt.
"But how does Kirillov make it pay?"

"Mituh!" (the contempt in the peasant's voice as he named the house porter was unmistakable) — "you can be sure he'll make it pay, Konstantin Dmitrievitch! He'll get his cut, however hard he has to squeeze for it. He has no mercy on a Christian. But Uncle Fokanitch" (as he called the old peasant Platon) — "do you think he'd skin a man alive? Where there's debt, he'll let a man off. He won't wring the last penny out. He's a man too."
"But why does he let anyone off?"

"Oh, well, of course, people are different. One man lives just for his own appetites and nothing else — like Mituh, he only thinks about filling his belly — but Fokanitch is a righteous man. He lives for his soul. He doesn't forget God."
"How thinks of God? How does he live for his soul?" Levin nearly shouted.
"Why, you know — in truth, in God's way. People are different. Take you now — you wouldn't wrong a man...."

"Yes, yes — goodbye!" said Levin, breathless with excitement, and turning around he took his stick and walked off briskly toward home. At the peasant's words — that Fokanitch lived for his soul, in truth, in God's way — undefined but momentous ideas seemed to burst out, as if they had been locked up, and they all rushed in one direction, swarming through his head and dazzling him with their light.

title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: Levin strode along the high road, absorbed less in his thoughts (he couldn't sort them out yet) than in a state of soul unlike anything he had known before.

The peasant's words had struck him like an electric shock, suddenly fusing into a single whole the whole swarm of disjointed, helpless, scattered thoughts that never left his mind. These thoughts had been there unnoticed even while he was talking about the land.
He sensed something new in his soul, and he tested it with joy, not yet knowing what it was.

"Not for his own wants, but for God. For what God? And could anything be said more senseless than what Fyodor said? He said one must not live for one's own wants — that is, not for what we understand, what we are drawn to, what we desire — but for something incomprehensible, for a God no one can grasp or even define. And what of it? Did I fail to understand those senseless words of Fyodor's? Did I, in understanding them, doubt their truth? Did I find them stupid, obscure, inexact? No. I understood him, and I understood him in exactly the sense he meant. I understood his words more fully and clearly than I understand anything else in life, and I have never doubted them, and I can never doubt them. And not only I — everyone, the whole world, understands nothing fully except this one thing, and about this one thing alone they never doubt and are always in agreement.

"And I was watching for miracles, complaining that no miracle came to convince me. A material miracle would have persuaded me. And here is a miracle — the only one possible, present always, surrounding me on every side — and I never noticed it!

"Fyodor says Kirillov lives for his belly. That makes sense, and it's rational. As rational creatures we can't do anything else but live for our belly.
