And then in the next breath the same Fyodor says one must not live for one's belly, but for truth, for God — and at a single hint I understand him. And I, and millions of people, men who lived ages ago and people living now — peasants, the poor in spirit and the learned, who have thought about it and written about it, in their obscure words saying the same thing — we are all agreed about this one thing: what we must live for, and what is good. I and all men have only one firm, incontestable, clear piece of knowledge, and that knowledge cannot be explained by reason — it stands outside reason, has no causes and can have no effects.
"If goodness has a cause, it is no longer goodness; if it has an effect, a reward, it is no longer goodness either. So goodness lies outside the chain of cause and effect.
"And yet I know it, and we all know it.
"What greater miracle could there be than that?

"Can I really have found the answer to it all? Can my suffering be over?" Levin thought as he strode along the dusty road, not noticing the heat or his weariness, feeling a release from long suffering. The feeling was so sweet it seemed to him impossible. He was breathless with emotion, unable to walk any further; he turned off the road into the woods and lay down in the shade of an aspen on the uncut grass. He pulled the hat off his hot head and propped himself on one elbow in the lush, feathery woodland grass.

"Yes, I have to make this clear to myself and understand," he thought, staring at the untrampled grass in front of him, following the movements of a green beetle that was climbing along a blade of couch-grass and lifting a leaf of goat-weed as it went. "What have I discovered?" he asked himself, bending the goat-weed leaf aside out of the beetle's way and twisting another blade above so that the beetle could cross over onto it. "What is it that's making me glad? What have I discovered?

"I haven't discovered anything. I've only realized what I knew already. I understand the force that gave me life in the past and gives me life now. I have been set free from falsehood; I have found the Master.

"I used to say that in my body, in the body of this grass and this beetle (there, she didn't take to the grass, she's spread her wings and flown off), a transformation of matter was going on according to physical, chemical, and physiological laws. And in all of us — as in the aspens and the clouds and the patches of mist — there was a process of evolution. Evolution from what? Into what? Eternal evolution and struggle — as if there could be any kind of direction or struggle in the eternal. And I was astonished that, no matter how hard I pushed my thinking along that road, I couldn't discover the meaning of life, the meaning of my own impulses and longings. Now I say I know the meaning of my life: 'To live for God, for my soul.' And this meaning, clear as it is, is mysterious and marvelous. Such, in fact, is the meaning of everything that exists. Yes, pride," he said to himself, rolling onto his stomach and starting to tie a loop out of blades of grass, trying not to break them.
"And not just pride of intellect — dullness of intellect. And most of all, the dishonesty of intellect. The cheating, knavish trickery of intellect — that's what it is," he said to himself.

And in his mind he ran briefly through the whole course of his ideas over the last two years, which had begun with the clear confrontation with death at the sight of his beloved brother hopelessly ill.

Then, for the first time grasping that for every person, himself included, nothing lay ahead but suffering, death, and oblivion, he had made up his mind that life could not be lived that way, and that he had to either interpret life so that it didn't present itself to him as some devil's nasty joke, or shoot himself.

But he had done neither — he had gone on living, thinking, and feeling, and had even married in that very stretch of time, and he had known many joys and had been happy, whenever he wasn't thinking about the meaning of his life.
What did that mean? It meant he had been living rightly, but thinking wrongly.

He had lived (without realizing it) on the spiritual truths he had drawn in with his mother's milk, but in his thinking he had not only failed to recognize those truths, he had deliberately ignored them.
Now it was clear to him that he could only live by the strength of the beliefs in which he had been raised.

"What would I have been, and how would I have spent my life, if I had not had those beliefs, if I had not known I must live for God and not for my own desires? I would have robbed and lied and killed. None of what makes the main happiness of my life would have existed for me." And with every effort of imagination he could not picture the brutal creature he himself would have been if he hadn't known what he was living for.

"I went looking for an answer to my question. And thought could not give an answer to my question — it is on a different scale from my question. The answer was given to me by life itself, in my knowledge of what is right and what is wrong. And that knowledge I did not arrive at in any way; it was given to me as it is given to everyone — _given_, because I could not have come by it from anywhere else.

"Where could I have got it? Could I have arrived by reason at the knowledge that I must love my neighbor and not oppress him? I was told it in childhood, and I believed it gladly, because they were telling me what was already in my soul. But who discovered it? Not reason. Reason discovered the struggle for existence, and the law that demands we oppress everyone who hinders the satisfaction of our desires. That is the deduction of reason. Love of one's neighbor reason could never have discovered — because it is irrational."

title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: And Levin remembered a scene he had recently witnessed between Dolly and her children. The children, left to themselves, had started cooking raspberries over the candles and squirting milk into each other's mouths with a syringe. Their mother, catching them at these pranks, started reminding them in Levin's presence of how much trouble their mischief gave the grown-ups, and that this trouble was all for their sake, and that if they broke the cups they would have nothing to drink their tea out of, and if they wasted the milk they would have nothing to eat and would die of hunger.

Levin had been struck by the passive, weary disbelief with which the children listened to what their mother said. They were simply irritated that their entertaining game had been interrupted, and they didn't believe a word of what she was saying. They couldn't believe it, because they couldn't take in the immensity of all they habitually enjoyed, and so they couldn't conceive that what they were destroying was the very thing they lived on.

"It all comes by itself," they thought, "and there's nothing interesting or important about it because it's always been like that and always will be. It's all the same anyway. We don't need to think about it — it's already there. But we want to come up with something new of our own. So we thought of putting raspberries in a cup and cooking them over a candle, and squirting milk straight into each other's mouths. That's fun, and something new, and not a bit worse than drinking out of cups."
"Isn't that exactly what we do, what I did, when we use reason to look for the meaning of the forces of nature and the meaning of human life?" he thought.

"Don't all the theories of philosophy do the same — try, by a path of thought that is foreign and unnatural to man, to bring him to a knowledge of what he has long known, and known so surely that without it he couldn't live at all? Isn't it clear, in the development of every philosopher's theory, that he knows the chief meaning of life beforehand, just as positively as the peasant Fyodor and not a bit more clearly, and that he is simply trying, by a dubious intellectual route, to get back to what everyone knows?

"Now then — leave the children to themselves to fetch their own dishes, milk the cows, and so on. Would they get into mischief? Why, they would die of hunger. Well then, leave us with our passions and thoughts, with no idea of the one God, the Creator, with no idea of what is right, with no idea of moral evil.
"Try building anything without those ideas.
"We only try to destroy them, because we're spiritually provided for. Exactly like the children.
"Where did I get that joyful knowledge, shared with the peasant, that alone gives peace to my soul? Where did I get it?

"Brought up with the idea of God, a Christian, my whole life filled with the spiritual blessings Christianity has given me, full of them and living on them — like the children I did not understand them, and I destroy, or try to destroy, what I live by. And as soon as a moment of real importance comes, like the children when they're cold and hungry, I turn to Him; and even less than the children get when their mother scolds them for their childish mischief, do I feel that my childish acts of wanton madness are counted against me.
"Yes — what I know, I know not by reason: it has been given to me, revealed to me, and I know it with my heart, by faith in the chief thing the church teaches.

"The church! The church!" Levin repeated to himself. He rolled over onto his other side and, leaning on his elbow, fell to gazing into the distance at a herd of cattle making their way down to the river.

"But can I believe everything the church teaches?" he thought, testing himself, calling up everything that could destroy his present peace of mind. He deliberately recalled all those doctrines of the church which had always seemed strangest to him and had always been stumbling blocks.
"The Creation? But how did I explain existence? By existence? By nothing? The devil and sin. But how do I explain evil? The atonement?
"But I know nothing — nothing — and I can know nothing but what has been told to me and to everyone else."
And it seemed to him that there was not a single article of faith in the church that could destroy the chief thing — faith in God, in goodness, as the one goal of human existence.

Under every article of faith of the church one could place the faith in the service of truth instead of one's own desires. And each doctrine not only left that faith intact, each doctrine seemed essential to completing that great miracle, continually present on earth, which made it possible for every person and millions of utterly different people — wise men and imbeciles, old men and children, all kinds of people, peasants, Lvov, Kitty, beggars and kings — to understand the same one thing perfectly, and so to build up that life of the soul which alone is worth living and alone is precious to us.

Lying on his back, he gazed up into the high, cloudless sky. "Don't I know that this is infinite space, and not a curved arch? But however I screw up my eyes and strain my sight, I cannot see it as not round and not bounded, and despite knowing about infinite space I am incontestably right when I see a solid blue dome, and more right than when I strain my eyes to see beyond it."
Levin stopped thinking, and only, as it were, listened to mysterious voices that seemed to speak joyfully and earnestly within him.
"Can this be faith?" he thought, afraid to believe in his own happiness. "My God, I thank Thee!" he said, swallowing his sobs and brushing the tears from his eyes with both hands.

title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: Levin looked ahead and saw a herd of cattle, and then he caught sight of his trap with Raven in the shafts, and the coachman, who, driving up to the herd, said something to the herdsman. Then he heard the clatter of the wheels and the snort of the well-fed horse close at hand. But he was so deep in his thoughts that he didn't even wonder why the coachman had come for him.
He only thought of it when the coachman had driven right up to him and shouted. "The mistress sent me. Your brother has come, and a gentleman with him."

Levin climbed into the trap and took the reins. As though just shaken out of sleep, it took him a long time to collect himself. He stared at the well-fed horse, flecked with lather between his haunches and at the neck where the harness rubbed, stared at Ivan the coachman sitting beside him, and remembered that he was expecting his brother, thought that his wife was probably uneasy at his long absence, and tried to guess who the visitor was that had come with his brother. And his brother and his wife and the unknown guest all seemed to him now quite different from before. He felt that from now on his relations with everyone would be different.

"With my brother there'll be none of that distance there's always been between us, there won't be any quarreling; with Kitty there will never be quarrels; with the visitor, whoever he is, I'll be friendly and pleasant; with the servants, with Ivan, everything will be different."

Holding tight on the stiff rein, reining in the good horse that snorted with impatience and seemed to be begging to be let go, Levin glanced at Ivan sitting next to him, not knowing what to do with his free hand, continually pressing down his shirt where it puffed out, and he tried to think of something to start a conversation with him about. He would have liked to say that Ivan had pulled the saddle girth up too high, but that was a reproach, and he was longing for friendly, warm talk. Nothing else came to mind.
"Your honor must keep to the right and look out for that stump," said the coachman, tugging at the rein Levin was holding.

"Please don't touch the rein and don't try to teach me!" said Levin, annoyed by the interference. Now, as always, interference made him angry, and he felt at once, with regret, how mistaken his assumption had been that his spiritual condition could instantly change the way he behaved when he was back in real life.
He was still a quarter of a mile from home when he saw Grisha and Tanya running to meet him.
"Uncle Kostya! Mamma's coming, and grandfather, and Sergey Ivanovitch, and someone else," they cried, scrambling up into the trap.
"Who is he?"
"An awfully terrible person! And he does this with his arms," said Tanya, standing up in the trap and imitating Katavasov.
"Old or young?" Levin asked, laughing, reminded of someone — he couldn't think who — by Tanya's performance.
"Oh, I hope he isn't tiresome," Levin thought.

As soon as he came around a bend in the road and saw the party coming, Levin recognized Katavasov in a straw hat, walking along swinging his arms exactly as Tanya had shown. Katavasov was very fond of debating metaphysics, having picked up his ideas from natural-science writers who had never studied metaphysics, and in Moscow lately Levin had had many arguments with him.
One of those arguments, one Katavasov had clearly considered himself the winner of, was the first thing Levin thought of as he recognized him.
"No, whatever happens, I won't argue and toss my ideas around lightly," he thought.
Getting out of the trap and greeting his brother and Katavasov, Levin asked about his wife.

"She has taken Mitya to Kolok" (a copse near the house). "She wanted to have him out there because it's so hot indoors," said Dolly. Levin had always advised his wife not to take the baby into the woods, thinking it unsafe, and he was not pleased to hear this.
"She rushes around from place to place with him," said the prince, smiling. "I told her to try putting him in the ice cellar."
"She meant to come to the bee-house. She thought you'd be there. We're going there now," said Dolly.
"Well, and what are you up to?" said Sergey Ivanovitch, dropping back from the others to walk beside him.
"Oh, nothing special. Busy as usual with the land," Levin answered. "And you — staying long? We've been expecting you for ages."
"Only a fortnight. I've a great deal to do in Moscow."

At those words the brothers' eyes met, and Levin, in spite of the wish he always had — stronger than ever just now — to be on warm and more open terms with his brother, felt awkward looking at him. He lowered his eyes and didn't know what to say.

Casting about for subjects of conversation that would please Sergey Ivanovitch and keep him off the Serbian war and the Slav question, which he had hinted at by mentioning what he had to do in Moscow, Levin began talking about Sergey Ivanovitch's book.
"So, have there been any reviews of your book?" he asked.
Sergey Ivanovitch smiled at how transparent the question was.

"No one's interested in that now, and I least of all," he said. "Just look, Darya Alexandrovna — we're going to have a shower," he added, pointing with a sunshade at the white rain clouds rising above the aspen tops.
And those words were enough to re-establish between the brothers that tone — not quite hostile, but chilly — which Levin had been so eager to avoid.
Levin went up to Katavasov.
"It was great of you to make up your mind to come," he said.
"I've been meaning to for ages. Now we'll have some real discussion — count on it. Have you been reading Spencer?"
"No, I haven't finished him," said Levin. "But I don't need him now."
"How's that? That's interesting. Why not?"
"I mean that I'm convinced I'll never find the answers to the questions that matter to me in Spencer or anyone like him. Now —"

But Katavasov's calm, good-humored expression suddenly struck him, and he felt such tenderness for his own happy mood — which he was clearly about to disturb with this conversation — that he remembered his resolution and stopped short.
"But we'll talk about it later," he added. "If we're going to the bee-house, this way — along this little path," he said, addressing them all.

Going along the narrow path to a little uncut meadow covered on one side with thick clumps of brilliant heart's-ease, among which here and there stood tall dark-green tufts of hellebore, Levin settled his guests in the dense, cool shade of the young aspens, on a bench and some stumps put there for guests at the bee-house who were afraid of the bees, and he went off himself to the hut to fetch bread, cucumbers, and fresh honey to treat them with.

Trying to keep his movements as deliberate as possible, listening to the bees that buzzed past him more and more often, he walked along the little path to the hut. At the entrance one bee hummed angrily, caught in his beard, but he carefully worked it free. Going into the shady outer room, he took his veil down from a peg on the wall, put it on, and, thrusting his hands into his pockets, walked into the fenced bee-garden where all the hives he knew so well stood in the midst of a closely mown plot in regular rows, fastened to posts with bast — the old stocks, each with its own history, and along the fence the younger swarms hived that year. In front of the openings of the hives, it made his eyes giddy to watch the bees and drones whirling around the same spot, while among them the working bees flew in and out with their spoils or in search of more, always in the same direction — into the woods toward the flowering lime trees and back to the hives.

His ears were filled with the constant hum in different keys — now the busy hum of a worker bee flying off quickly, now the blaring of a lazy drone, and the agitated buzz of the sentry bees on guard, protecting their property from intruders and preparing to sting. On the far side of the fence, the old beekeeper was shaving a hoop for a tub, and he didn't see Levin. Levin stood still in the middle of the beehives and did not call to him.

He was glad of a chance to be alone and recover from the influence of ordinary life, which had already darkened his happy mood. He thought how he had already had time to lose his temper with Ivan, to be cool with his brother, and to talk flippantly with Katavasov.

"Can it really have been only a passing mood — will it pass and leave no trace?" he thought. But the same instant, returning to his mood, he felt with delight that something new and important had happened to him. Real life had only briefly clouded over the spiritual peace he had found, but it was still intact within him.

Just as the bees, whirling around him, now menacing him and pulling at his attention, kept him from full physical peace, forcing him to restrain his movements to avoid them, so the small concerns that had swarmed around him from the moment he climbed into the trap had cramped his spiritual freedom; but that lasted only as long as he was among them. Just as his bodily strength was unaffected in spite of the bees, so too was the spiritual strength he had only just become aware of.

title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: "Do you know, Kostya, who Sergey Ivanovitch traveled with on his way here?" said Dolly, doling out cucumbers and honey to the children. "With Vronsky! He's on his way to Serbia."
"And not alone — he's taking a whole squadron at his own expense," added Katavasov.
"That suits him," said Levin. "Are volunteers still going out, then?" he added, glancing at Sergey Ivanovitch.
Sergey Ivanovitch didn't answer. He was carefully using a blunt knife to lift a live bee, smeared with sticky honey, out of a cup full of white comb.
"I'd say so! You should have seen what was going on at the station yesterday!" said Katavasov, biting into a cucumber with a juicy crunch.

"Well, what's one to make of it? For pity's sake, do explain to me, Sergey Ivanovitch — where are all these volunteers going, and who are they fighting with?" asked the old prince, plainly picking up a conversation that had started in Levin's absence.
"With the Turks," Sergey Ivanovitch answered, smiling calmly as he lifted out the bee — dark with honey, helplessly kicking — and set it down with the knife on a stout aspen leaf.
"And who declared war on the Turks? Ivan Ivanovitch Ragozov and Countess Lidia Ivanovna, with Madame Stahl's help?"
"No one has declared war, but people sympathize with their neighbors' suffering and want to help them," said Sergey Ivanovitch.

"But the prince isn't talking about helping," said Levin, coming to his father-in-law's defense, "he's talking about war. The prince says that private citizens can't take part in war without the government's permission."
"Kostya, watch out — that's a bee! Really, they'll sting us!" said Dolly, waving a wasp away.
"That's not a bee, it's a wasp," said Levin.
"All right, well, then — what's your own theory?" Katavasov said to Levin with a smile, clearly challenging him to a debate. "Why have private citizens no right to do it?"

"Well, my theory is this: on one side, war is such a beastly, cruel, and horrible thing that no man, let alone a Christian, can take on himself personally the responsibility of starting a war; only a government can do that — it's the body called to do it, and is dragged into war inevitably. On the other hand, both political science and common sense tell us that in matters of state, and especially in matters of war, private citizens must give up their personal will."
Sergey Ivanovitch and Katavasov both had replies ready, and both started speaking at the same time.
"But the point is, my dear fellow, that there may be cases where the government does not carry out the will of its citizens, and then the public asserts its will," said Katavasov.
But Sergey Ivanovitch clearly didn't approve of this answer. His brow tightened at Katavasov's words and he said something different.

"You aren't framing the matter properly. This is not a question of declaring war — it is simply the expression of a human, Christian feeling. Our brothers, one with us in religion and in blood, are being massacred. Even supposing they weren't our brothers or fellow Christians, but simply children, women, old people — feeling is stirred up, and Russians go willingly to help put a stop to these atrocities. Imagine if you were walking down the street and saw drunken men beating a woman or a child — I don't think you'd stop to ask whether war had been declared on the men; you'd throw yourself on them and protect the victim."
"But I wouldn't kill them," said Levin.
"Yes you would."

"I don't know. If I saw something like that, I might give way to the impulse of the moment, but I can't tell beforehand. And no such momentary impulse exists, or can exist, in the case of the oppression of the Slav peoples."

"It may not exist for you; but for others it does," said Sergey Ivanovitch, frowning with displeasure. "There are still traditions alive among the people of Slavs of the true faith suffering under the yoke of the 'unclean sons of Hagar.' The people have heard of their brothers' suffering, and they have spoken."
"Perhaps so," Levin said evasively, "but I don't see it. I'm one of the people myself, and I don't feel it."

"And here am I too," said the old prince. "I've been living abroad and reading the papers, and I have to admit, up until the time of the Bulgarian atrocities, I couldn't make out why all the Russians were suddenly so fond of their Slav brethren, while I didn't feel the slightest affection for them. I was very upset, thought I was a monster, or that it was the influence of Carlsbad on me. But since I've been back here, my mind has been put at ease. I see there are people besides me who are interested only in Russia, not in their Slav brethren. Konstantin here, for one."
"Personal opinions count for nothing in a case like this," said Sergey Ivanovitch; "it's not a question of personal opinions when all of Russia — the entire people — has expressed its will."
"But excuse me, I don't see that. The people don't know anything about it, if it comes to that," said the old prince.

"Oh, papa — how can you say that? And last Sunday in church?" said Dolly, listening to the conversation. "Please give me a cloth," she said to the old beekeeper, who was watching the children with a smile. "It can't be that everyone —"

"What was it in church on Sunday? The priest had been told to read it. He read it. They didn't understand a word. Then they were told there would be a collection for a pious cause; well, they pulled out their halfpennies and gave them, but what for they couldn't say."

"The people can't help knowing; the sense of their own destiny is always alive in the people, and at moments like the present that sense finds its voice," said Sergey Ivanovitch with conviction, glancing at the old beekeeper.

The handsome old man, with a black grizzled beard and thick silvery hair, stood motionless, holding a cup of honey, looking down from his tall height at the gentlefolk with friendly serenity, obviously understanding nothing of their talk and not interested in trying to.
"That's so, no doubt," he said, giving a meaningful nod at Sergey Ivanovitch's words.

"Then ask him. He knows nothing about it and thinks nothing," said Levin. "Have you heard about the war, Mihalitch?" he said, turning to him. "About what they read in church? What do you make of it? Should we be fighting for the Christians?"

"What's there for us to think? Alexander Nikolaevitch our Emperor has thought for us; he thinks for us in everything. It's clearer for him to see. Shall I bring some more bread? Some for the little lad?" he said, turning to Darya Alexandrovna and pointing to Grisha, who had finished his crust.

"I don't need to ask," said Sergey Ivanovitch. "We have seen, and we go on seeing, hundreds upon hundreds of people who give up everything to serve a just cause — they come from every part of Russia, and they say openly and clearly what they're doing it for. They bring their halfpennies or go themselves, and they say plainly what for. What does it mean?"

"It means, in my view," said Levin, getting heated, "that among eighty million people there can always be found, not hundreds as now, but tens of thousands of people who have lost their place — ne'er-do-wells, always ready to go anywhere — to Pogatchev's bands, to Khiva, to Serbia —"

"I tell you, it is not a matter of hundreds and it is not a matter of ne'er-do-wells, but the best representatives of the people!" said Sergey Ivanovitch, with as much irritation as if he were defending the last penny of his fortune. "And what of the subscriptions? In this case it's a whole people directly expressing its will."

"That word 'people' is so vague," said Levin. "Parish clerks, schoolteachers, and maybe one peasant in a thousand know what it's all about. The rest of the eighty million, like Mihalitch, far from expressing their will, haven't the faintest idea what there is for them to express a will about. What right do we have to say this is the will of the people?"

title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: Sergey Ivanovitch, practiced in argument, didn't reply but at once turned the conversation to another angle.

"Oh, if you want to learn the spirit of the people by arithmetic, of course it's very difficult to get at. And voting hasn't been introduced among us and can't be — it doesn't express the will of the people; but there are other ways of reaching it. You can feel it in the air, feel it in your heart. I won't speak of those deep currents stirring in the still ocean of the people, currents which are obvious to every unbiased man; let's just look at society in the narrow sense. All the most different sections of the educated public, hostile to one another before, are merged in one. Every division is at an end, every public organ says the same thing again and again, all of them feel the great current that has caught them up and is carrying them in one direction."
"Yes, all the newspapers do say the same thing," said the prince. "That's true. But so do all the frogs croak the same thing before a storm. You can't hear anything for them."

"Frogs or no frogs, I'm not the editor of a paper and I don't want to defend them; but I'm speaking of the unanimity in the world of thought," said Sergey Ivanovitch, addressing his brother. Levin would have answered, but the old prince broke in.

"Well, about that unanimity, that's another matter, you might say," said the prince. "There's my son-in-law, Stepan Arkadyevitch, you know him. He's got a place now on the committee of some commission, I don't remember which. Only there's nothing to do in it — well, Dolly, it's no secret — and a salary of eight thousand. Try asking him whether the post is of any use; he'll prove to you it's absolutely essential. And he's a truthful man too — but there's no refusing to believe in the usefulness of eight thousand roubles."
"Yes — he asked me to pass on a message to Darya Alexandrovna about that post," said Sergey Ivanovitch reluctantly, feeling the prince's remark was poorly timed.

"It's the same with the unanimity of the press. It was explained to me: as soon as there's war, their revenues are doubled. How can they help believing in the destinies of the people and the Slav races and all that?"
"I don't care for many of the papers, but that's unjust," said Sergey Ivanovitch.

"I'd only make one condition," the old prince went on. "Alphonse Karr said a capital thing before the war with Prussia: 'You think war is inevitable? Very good. Let everyone who advocates war be put into a special regiment of advance guards, to lead every storm, every attack — lead them all.'"
"A nice lot the editors would make," said Katavasov, with a roar of laughter as he pictured the editors he knew in this picked legion.
"But they'd run," said Dolly. "They'd only be in the way."
"Oh, if they ran, then we'd have grape-shot or Cossacks with whips behind them," said the prince.
"But that's a joke, and a poor one, if you'll forgive me, prince," said Sergey Ivanovitch.
"I don't see why it was a joke, that —" Levin started, but Sergey Ivanovitch cut him off.

"Every member of society is called on to do his own particular work," he said. "And men of thought are doing their work when they give voice to public opinion. And the single-hearted and full expression of public opinion is the service the press performs, and it's a thing to rejoice over besides. Twenty years ago we would have kept silent; now we have heard the voice of the Russian people, ready to rise as one man and ready to sacrifice itself for its oppressed brethren — that is a great step, and a proof of strength."

"But it's not just making a sacrifice — it's killing Turks," Levin said timidly. "The people make sacrifices and are ready to make sacrifices for their souls, but not for murder," he added, instinctively connecting the conversation with the ideas that had been filling his mind.
"For their souls? That's an extremely puzzling phrase for a natural-science man, you understand. What sort of thing is the soul?" said Katavasov with a smile.
"Oh, you know!"
"No, by God, I haven't the faintest idea!" said Katavasov, with another roar of laughter.
"'I bring not peace, but a sword,' says Christ," Sergey Ivanovitch chimed in, quoting just as simply as if it were the easiest thing in the world the very passage that had always puzzled Levin most.
"That's so, no doubt," the old man repeated again. He was standing nearby, and answered a chance glance turned in his direction.
"Ah, my dear fellow — you're defeated, utterly defeated!" cried Katavasov good-humoredly.
Levin reddened with annoyance, not at being defeated, but at having failed to hold himself in check and at having been drawn into argument.
"No, I can't argue with them," he thought; "they're wearing impenetrable armor, while I'm naked."

He could see that there was no way to convince his brother and Katavasov, and even less chance of his own agreeing with them. What they were defending was exactly that pride of intellect which had almost been his ruin. He could not admit that some dozens of men, his brother among them, had the right — on the basis of what they were told by a few hundred glib volunteers swarming to the capital — to say that they and the newspapers were expressing the will and feeling of the people, a feeling expressed in vengeance and murder. He could not admit it, because he didn't see the expression of any such feelings in the people he lived among, nor did he find them in himself (and he could not help considering himself one of the people who made up the Russian nation), and most of all because he, like the people, did not know and could not know what was for the general good, though he knew beyond doubt that this general good could only be reached by strict observance of the law of right and wrong that had been revealed to every man, and therefore he could not wish for war or advocate it for any general aims whatever. He said what Mihalitch said and what the people said, who had expressed their feeling in the old story of the Varyagi's invitation: "Be princes and rule over us. We promise complete submission gladly. All the labor, all the humiliations, all the sacrifices we take upon ourselves; but we will not judge and decide." And now, according to Sergey Ivanovitch's account, the people had given up that privilege they had bought at such a costly price.

He wanted to say too that if public opinion were an infallible guide, then why weren't revolutions and the commune just as legitimate as the movement on behalf of the Slav peoples? But these were thoughts that could settle nothing. One thing could be seen beyond doubt — at this very moment the discussion was annoying Sergey Ivanovitch, and so it was wrong to keep it up. And Levin stopped speaking and then drew his guests' attention to the fact that the storm clouds were gathering and they had better head home before it rained.

title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: The old prince and Sergey Ivanovitch got into the trap and drove off; the rest of the party hurried home on foot.

But the storm clouds, turning white and then black, came down so quickly that they had to quicken their pace to get home before the rain. The leading clouds, low and black as soot-laden smoke, rushed across the sky with extraordinary speed. They were still two hundred paces from home when a gust of wind blew up, and any moment now the downpour might come.

The children ran ahead with frightened and gleeful shrieks. Darya Alexandrovna, struggling painfully with skirts that clung around her legs, was no longer walking but running, her eyes fixed on the children. The men, holding their hats on, strode along beside her with long strides. They were just at the steps when a big drop fell with a splash on the edge of the iron gutter. The children, and the grown-ups after them, ran into the shelter of the house, chattering cheerfully.
"Katerina Alexandrovna?" Levin asked Agafea Mihalovna, who met them in the hall with kerchiefs and rugs.
"We thought she was with you," she said.
"And Mitya?"
"In the copse, he must be, and the nurse with him."
Levin snatched up the rugs and ran toward the copse.

In that brief stretch of time the storm clouds had moved on, covering the sun so completely that it was dark as an eclipse. Stubbornly, as though insisting on its rights, the wind held Levin back, and tearing the leaves and flowers off the lime trees and stripping the white birch branches into a strange, unseemly nakedness, it bent everything sideways — acacias, flowers, burdocks, long grass, and the tops of trees. The peasant girls working in the garden ran shrieking for shelter in the servants' quarters. The streaming rain had already flung its white veil over the distant woods and half the nearby fields, and was sweeping down quickly upon the copse. The wet smell of rain bursting into tiny droplets was in the air.

Holding his head bent before him, struggling with the wind that tried to tear the wraps from him, Levin was moving up to the copse and had just caught sight of something white behind the oak tree when there was a sudden flash, the whole earth seemed on fire, and the vault of heaven seemed to crash overhead. Opening his blinded eyes, Levin stared through the thick veil of rain that now separated him from the copse, and to his horror the first thing he saw was the green crown of the familiar oak tree in the middle of the copse uncannily shifting its position. "Can it have been struck?" Levin barely had time to think, when, moving faster and faster, the oak tree vanished behind the other trees, and he heard the crash of the great tree falling onto them.
The flash of lightning, the crack of thunder, and the instant chill that ran through him all merged for Levin into a single feeling of terror.
"My God! My God! Not on them!" he said.

And though he realized at once how senseless his prayer was that they should not have been killed by the oak which had already fallen, he repeated it, knowing he could do nothing better than utter this senseless prayer.
Running up to the place where they usually sat, he didn't find them there.

They were at the other end of the copse, under an old lime tree, calling him. Two figures in dark dresses (they had been light summer dresses when they set out) stood bending over something. It was Kitty with the nurse. The rain was already letting up and it was beginning to grow light when Levin reached them. The nurse was dry on the lower part of her dress, but Kitty was drenched through, and her soaked clothes clung to her. Even though the rain was over, they still stood in the same position they had been in when the storm broke. Both were bending over a perambulator with a green umbrella.
"Alive? Unhurt? Thank God!" he said, splashing with his soaked boots through the standing water as he ran up to them.
Kitty's rosy, wet face turned toward him, and she smiled at him timidly from under her shapeless, sopping hat.
"Aren't you ashamed of yourself? I can't think how you can be so reckless!" he said angrily to his wife.
"It really wasn't my fault. We were just about to leave when he kicked up such a fuss we had to change him. We were just —" Kitty began, defending herself.
Mitya was unhurt, dry, and still fast asleep.
"Well, thank God! I don't know what I'm saying!"

They gathered up the baby's wet things; the nurse picked the baby up and carried him. Levin walked beside his wife, repentant for having been angry, and squeezed her hand whenever the nurse wasn't looking.

title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: All through that day, in the wildly varied conversations he took part in — only with the top layer of his mind, as it were — and in spite of the disappointment of not finding the change in himself he had expected, Levin had been joyfully aware all along of the fullness of his heart.

After the rain it was too wet for a walk; besides, the storm clouds still hung about the horizon and were gathering here and there, black and thundery, along the rim of the sky. The whole party spent the rest of the day in the house.
No more arguments broke out; on the contrary, after dinner everyone was in the most pleasant mood.

First Katavasov amused the ladies with his original jokes, which always charmed people on first acquaintance. Then Sergey Ivanovitch got him going about the very interesting observations he had made on the habits and lives of common houseflies. Sergey Ivanovitch was in good spirits too, and at tea his brother drew him out on his views of the future of the Eastern question, and he spoke so simply and so well that everyone listened eagerly.
Only Kitty did not hear all of it — she was called away to give Mitya his bath.
A few minutes after Kitty left the room, she sent for Levin to come to the nursery.

Leaving his tea, regretfully interrupting the interesting conversation, and at the same time uneasily wondering why he had been summoned, since this only happened on important occasions, Levin went to the nursery.

Although he had been very interested in Sergey Ivanovitch's view of the new epoch in history that would be created by the liberation of forty million Slavs acting together with Russia — an idea entirely new to him — and although he was uneasily wondering why Kitty had sent for him, as soon as he was out of the drawing-room and alone his mind reverted straight back to the morning's thoughts. And all those theories about the significance of the Slav element in the history of the world seemed so trivial compared to what was going on in his own soul that he instantly forgot it all and fell back into the same frame of mind he had been in that morning.

He did not, as he had at other times, retrace the whole train of thought — he didn't need to. He fell back at once into the feeling that had guided him, which was bound up with those thoughts, and he found that feeling in his soul even stronger and more defined than before. He did not, as he had had to with previous attempts to find comforting arguments, need to revive a whole chain of thought to recover the feeling. Now, on the contrary, the feeling of joy and peace was sharper than ever, and thought could not keep pace with feeling.

He crossed the terrace and looked at two stars that had come out in the darkening sky, and suddenly he remembered. "Yes, when I was looking up at the sky, I thought that the dome I see is not a deception, and then I thought of something — I shied away from something," he mused. "But whatever it was, there's no disproving it. I only have to think, and it will all come clear."

Just as he was going into the nursery he remembered what it was he had shied away from. It was this: if the chief proof of the Divinity is His revelation of what is right, why is this revelation confined to the Christian church alone? What relation to this revelation do the beliefs of the Buddhists, the Mohammedans — who also preached and did good — bear?
It seemed to him that he had an answer to this question; but he didn't have time to formulate it to himself before he stepped into the nursery.

Kitty was standing with her sleeves rolled up over the baby in the bath. Hearing her husband's step, she turned toward him, calling him over with her smile. With one hand she was supporting the fat baby, who was floating and sprawling on his back, while with the other she squeezed the sponge over him.
"Come, look, look!" she said when her husband came up to her. "Agafea Mihalovna's right. He knows us!"
That day Mitya had given unmistakable, undeniable signs of recognizing all his friends.

As soon as Levin came up to the bath, the experiment was tried, and it was completely successful. The cook, called in for this purpose, bent down over the baby. He frowned and shook his head disapprovingly. Kitty bent down to him, and he gave her a beaming smile, propped his little hands on the sponge and chirped, making such an odd little contented sound with his lips that Kitty and the nurse weren't alone in their delight. Levin too was surprised and delighted.
The baby was lifted out of the bath, doused with water, wrapped in towels, dried, and after a piercing scream handed to his mother.

"Well, I'm glad you're starting to love him," said Kitty to her husband, when she had settled herself comfortably in her usual place with the baby at her breast. "I'm so glad. It was beginning to distress me. You said you didn't feel anything for him."
"No — did I say that? I only said I was disappointed."
"What — disappointed in him?"
"Not disappointed in him, but in my own feeling. I'd been expecting more. I'd expected a rush of some new, wonderful emotion to come over me as a surprise. And instead of that — distaste, pity —"
She listened attentively, watching him over the baby, while she slid the rings she had taken off for the bath back onto her slender fingers.
"And most of all, there was far more anxiety and pity than pleasure. Today, after that fright in the storm, I understand how much I love him."
Kitty's smile was radiant.

"Were you very frightened?" she said. "I was too — but I feel it more now that it's over. I'm going to go look at the oak tree. How nice Katavasov is! And what a happy day we've had altogether. And you're so pleasant with Sergey Ivanovitch, when you want to be. Well, go back to them. It's always so hot and steamy in here after the bath."

title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: Leaving the nursery and finding himself alone again, Levin went straight back to the thought in which something was still unclear.
Instead of going into the drawing-room, where he could hear voices, he stopped on the terrace and, leaning his elbows on the parapet, gazed up at the sky.

It was quite dark now, and in the south, where he was looking, there were no clouds. The storm had drifted off to the other side of the sky, and there were flashes of lightning and distant rumbles of thunder from that quarter. Levin listened to the steady drip from the lime trees in the garden and looked at the triangle of stars he knew so well, and the Milky Way with its branches running through the middle. With every flash of lightning the Milky Way, and even the brightest stars, vanished, but the moment the lightning died out they reappeared in their places, as though some hand had flung them back with careful aim.

"Well, what is it that's troubling me?" Levin said to himself, feeling already that the solution to his difficulties was waiting in his soul, even if he didn't yet know what it was. "Yes, the one unmistakable, incontestable manifestation of the Divinity is the law of right and wrong, which has come into the world through revelation, and which I feel in myself, and in recognizing which — whether I will or not — I am made one with other people in one body of believers, which is called the church. But the Jews, the Mohammedans, the Confucians, the Buddhists — what about them?" he asked himself the question he had been afraid to face. "Can hundreds of millions of people be deprived of that highest blessing without which life has no meaning?" He paused for a moment, then corrected himself. "But what am I even asking?" he said to himself. "I'm asking about the relation to Divinity of all the different religions of all humanity. I'm asking about God's universal manifestation to the whole world, with all those misty blurs. What am I doing? To me personally, to my heart, a knowledge has been revealed beyond all doubt and beyond the reach of reason, and here I am stubbornly trying to put that knowledge into words and reason.

"Don't I know that the stars don't move?" he asked himself, looking at a bright planet that had shifted to the top twig of the birch tree. "But looking at the motion of the stars, I can't picture the rotation of the earth, and I'm right to say the stars move.

"And could the astronomers have understood or calculated anything if they had had to take into account all the complicated and varied motions of the earth? All the marvelous conclusions they have reached about the distances, weights, motions, and deflections of the heavenly bodies are founded only on the apparent motions of the heavenly bodies around a stationary earth — on the very motion I see in front of me right now, the motion that has been there for millions of people through long ages, and was and always will be the same, and can always be relied on. And just as the astronomers' conclusions would have been empty and uncertain if not founded on observations of the visible sky in relation to a single meridian and a single horizon, so my conclusions would be empty and uncertain if they weren't founded on that conception of right which has been and always will be the same for all people, which has been revealed to me as a Christian, and which can always be trusted in my soul. The question of other religions and their relation to the Divinity I have no right to decide, and no way of deciding."
"Oh, you haven't gone in yet?" he heard Kitty's voice all at once as she came the same way toward the drawing-room.
"What is it? You aren't upset about anything?" she said, looking carefully at his face in the starlight.

But she would not have been able to see his face if a flash of lightning hadn't hidden the stars and lit it up for her. In that flash she saw his face clearly, and seeing that he was calm and happy, she smiled at him.
"She understands," he thought; "she knows what I'm thinking about. Should I tell her, or not? Yes — I'll tell her." But at the moment he was about to speak, she began.

"Kostya — do something for me," she said. "Go into the corner room and see if they've made it up properly for Sergey Ivanovitch. I can't very well do it myself. See if they've put the new washstand in there."
"Very well, I'll go right away," said Levin, standing up and kissing her.
"No — I'd better not speak of it," he thought when she had gone in ahead of him. "It's a secret for me alone, of vital importance to me, and not to be put into words.

"This new feeling has not changed me, has not made me happy and enlightened all of a sudden, the way I'd dreamed — just like with the feeling for my child. There was no surprise about it either. Whether it's faith or not, I don't know — but this feeling has come in just as imperceptibly, through suffering, and has taken firm root in my soul.

"I'll go on the same way — losing my temper with Ivan the coachman, falling into pointless arguments, expressing my opinions tactlessly; there will still be the same wall between the holy of holies of my soul and other people, even my wife; I'll still go on scolding her out of my own fear, and being remorseful about it; I'll still be just as unable to understand by reason why I pray, and I'll still go on praying. But my life now — my whole life, apart from anything that may happen to me — every minute of it is no longer meaningless as it was before, but has the positive meaning of goodness, which I have the power to put into it."
